sample.title: CI: replace per-package test steps with pnpm -r --parallel run verify
sample.body:
## Problem

The `test.yml` workflow hardcodes which packages get tested. It currently runs unit tests with coverage for only 4 packages:

- `@lucasschirm/sal-claude-session-parser`
- `@lucasschirm/sal-sync`
- `@lucasschirm/claude-session-sync`
- `site`

The 4 analytics packages are **not tested in CI** despite having full vitest suites:

| Package | Test files | `test:coverage` | Run in CI? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `db-core` | 12 | yes | no |
| `db` | 32 | yes | no |
| `transformer` | 12 | yes | no |
| `sync-core` | 8 | yes | no |

That's 64 test files — including the ingestion orchestrator, rollup reconciliation, reprocessing engine, schema parity, and pipeline integration tests — none of which run in CI.

Every new package added to the workspace will silently have no CI coverage unless someone remembers to add a step to `test.yml`.

## Proposed solution

The root `package.json` already has a `verify` script:

```json
"verify": "pnpm -r build && pnpm -r --parallel run verify"
```

Every workspace package defines its own `verify` script (`typecheck && lint && test`). CI should run `pnpm run verify` (or `pnpm -r --parallel run verify` after a build step) instead of enumerating individual packages. This lets each package decide what needs to be verified and automatically picks up new packages added to the workspace.

### Considerations

- **Coverage thresholds**: The current `test.yml` enforces coverage thresholds via per-package `test:coverage` scripts. The `verify` scripts run `test` (not `test:coverage`). We need to decide whether coverage should be enforced in CI or left as a local concern. Options:
  1. Change each package's `verify` to run `test:coverage` instead of `test`
  2. Keep `verify` as `test` and add a separate coverage step
  3. Drop CI coverage enforcement (rely on local + pre-commit)
- **E2E tests**: The site Playwright E2E tests need browser installation and are slow. They should probably remain a separate CI step rather than part of `verify`.
- **Parallelism**: `pnpm -r --parallel run verify` runs all packages concurrently. The `db` package has perf tests that take ~15-20s and pipeline tests; parallelism should be fine but worth confirming no shared-state conflicts (e.g. port collisions, temp files).
- **Build step**: `verify` already includes `pnpm -r build` at the front, so the build-then-verify flow is self-contained.

### Suggested `test.yml` structure

```yaml
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [22, 24]
    steps:
      - checkout
      - setup pnpm + node
      - pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - pnpm run verify          # builds all, then runs each package's verify in parallel
      - upload coverage artifacts (if coverage is kept)

  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: verify
    steps:
      - checkout
      - setup pnpm + node
      - pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - pnpm -r build
      - playwright install
      - pnpm --filter site test:e2e
```

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All 8 workspace packages are verified in CI (typecheck + lint + test)
- [ ] New packages added to the workspace are automatically picked up by CI
- [ ] No hardcoded per-package test steps in `test.yml`
- [ ] E2E tests remain a separate step (browser install, slower)
- [ ] Coverage enforcement decision is documented

sample.title: Recover an accepted Standard answer without resubmission
sample.body:
## Parent decision

[Standard-first transaction and recovery contract](https://github.com/rookslog/chatgpt-research-adapter/issues/58).

## What to build

Public typed status/collect resumes the accepted Standard conversation after restart and publishes its bound answer without a new submission.

## Acceptance

- Restart from persisted acceptance and recover only that conversation/turn.
- Intent-only remains uncertain; collection failures preserve the previously established remote effect.
- Collection has no prompt/submission authority. Duplicate collection is idempotent; conflicting identities or digests require attention.
- Interrupted publication and historical receipts use explicit, verified successor semantics.
- Tests cover accepted restart, interruption, duplicate completion, wrong turn and legacy intent-only using a read-only fake reader with a send trap.

## Blocked by

The first transaction's receipt contract and implementation (native edge added after creation).


## Approved workflow and limits

Owner approved the Standard-first recommendations in the September 6 conversation; decisions40/58 are closed with the approval. Verify-only model behavior, exclusive submission control, typed recovery, current dependency-free gates. Test design Astra Medium/High; fresh isolated test author Astra Medium/Low; different fresh Astra Low code author. Root freezes RED tests and independently verifies GREEN plus relevant regressions. No live provider calls, upstream installation changes, new dependencies, commits, publication or general scheduler/MCP implementation. Material scope expansion remains a new decision.

## Verification

Run the behavior-specific RED/GREEN checks, unchanged frozen-test hashes, npm test, check:authority, check:requirements, check:syntax, and package dry-run as appropriate to the slice. Preserve production source/receipt authority and traceability; revise expected inventory/digests only for reviewed authorized changes, never disable enforcement. Source identities and qualification limits must be recorded.

sample.title: shipyard: tell and compact report 'the child is gone' for a terminal that is only absent on the backend they resolved
sample.body:
Two places now read absence-on-the-resolved-backend as the child being gone, which is the inference
#130 just refused one level up.

`SKILL.md` documents `shipyard-tell.sh`'s exit 3 as:

> Exit 3 = no live terminal for that slot (the child is gone)

and `shipyard-tell.sh` / `shipyard-compact.sh` print matching messages. But `shipyard_target`
resolves against whatever backend *this process* picked, and `SHIPYARD_BACKEND=auto` decides per
process by probing the agterm control socket. During a blip the answer is "no terminal on the
backend I happened to resolve", not "the child is gone".

## Why it matters

The supervising agent acts on this. Told a child is gone, the reasonable next moves are to tear the
slot down or relaunch it — against a child that is mid-review and alive in the other backend. That
is the #61 harm (supervision lost over live work) reached through a different door, and with a
destructive action at the end of it rather than merely silence.

## Suggested fix

The cheap, honest half: reword to "no live terminal for that slot **on the backend this run
resolved**", in `SKILL.md` and in both scripts' messages, and point at the `🛑 NO SIGNAL` vocabulary
#130 introduced so the reader knows the distinction exists.

The fuller half, if it proves worth it: have `tell`/`compact` apply the same corroboration the
report now does — a slot with a launch record and a live worktree, whose terminal cannot be found,
is unresolved rather than gone. That overlaps the per-slot launch record proposed in the pin-staleness
issue, so the two are best done together.

Found by the review battery on #130 (`sweep-docs`).

sample.title: Post-merge: centralize dispatch ack/idle timeout governance (leader-ack brittleness + §6 idle + pre-auto-merge head re-confirm)
sample.body:
## Post-merge design work: centralize dispatch ack/idle timeout governance in the §6 monitor

**Status:** Deferred, non-blocking for the autonomous-dispatch integration→master merge. Surfaced during the tizonia e2e verification run. To be tackled as its own brainstorm→spec→plan cycle after the merge, and **required before Claude Deck runs genuinely unattended against a live roadmap at scale.**

### Design docs (reasoning lives with the code)
- `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-06-dispatch-open-finding-leader-ack-timeout.md` — the leader-ack-gate brittleness finding (primary).
- `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-05-dispatch-open-finding-stale-ready-state.md` — sibling deferred finding (stale `ready_for_review` on a post-promotion red head).

### The theme
Three deferred items share one root: **wait/timeout decisions are scattered (in owner prompts, or absent) instead of governed centrally by the brain's §6 monitor.** They should be designed together:

1. **Leader-ack gate brittleness** (primary). A hard "leader must ack before work" gate strands work when the leader is briefly unresponsive (observed: T-S8, leader answered ~3min late, owner had already escalated). The wait/give-up logic currently lives in the *owner's prompt* (improvised, inconsistent). Move it into §6 with configurable, **pipeline-tiered** timeouts + a **leader-nudge-before-escalate** step.
   - **Critical constraint:** the fix must be tiered by pipeline, NOT a uniform softening. Code-pipeline ack is an early-plan-check (PR still human-reviewed → may proceed-after-timeout); design-pipeline ack **is** the C1 human-approval substitute (must strictly escalate, never proceed unreviewed). A uniform "soften the gate" would reopen C1.

2. **§6 reachable-but-idle monitor** (deferred since Phase A). The owner/leader "reachable but idle" nudge/escalate path is still a stub — only the offline fast-path is implemented. This is the same machinery the ack-timeout work needs (last-activity plumbing + nudge-before-escalate), so build them together.

3. **Stale `ready_for_review` on post-promotion red head** (sibling finding). Revisit **before enabling `merge_policy=auto`** — at minimum re-confirm CI-green on the current head immediately before an auto-merge.

### Why deferred (not a merge blocker)
- All three are "works but fragile / UX-honesty" issues, not correctness or safety defects in the core loop.
- The e2e run gated the merge on human-merge-only operation, where a human is watching and failures are visible+recoverable (escalated→pending + Retry). None can cause a bad merge under that posture.
- The dangerous versions (silent stranding at scale; auto-merging a stale-green PR) only bite under genuinely-unattended and/or `merge_policy=auto` operation — which is itself post-merge.

### Suggested sequencing
Brainstorm the three together as "centralize ack/idle timeout governance + pre-auto-merge head re-confirm," since they share the §6 monitor and last-activity plumbing. Item 3 additionally gates enabling `merge_policy=auto`.

sample.title: run_tests(mode="PlayMode") hangs the Editor on Linux/Vulkan — no test starts, futex_do_wait
sample.body:
## Summary

`run_tests(mode="PlayMode")` never starts any test and **hangs the Unity Editor**. `EditMode`
runs are fine, and entering Play Mode manually is fine. Only the PlayMode *test run* is
affected.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| MCPForUnity | v10.1.2 (`com.coplaydev.unity-mcp`, git `#v10.1.2`) |
| Server | `mcpforunityserver==10.1.2`, HTTP transport, `127.0.0.1:8790`, `--project-scoped-tools` |
| Unity | 2022.3.22f1 (`887be4894c44`) |
| OS | Arch Linux, kernel 7.2.3 |
| Graphics | Vulkan (`-force-vulkan`), NVIDIA RTX 3060, driver 610.57.04 |
| Project | VRChat avatar project: SDK 3.5.0, NDMF 1.14.3, Modular Avatar 1.17.1, VRCFury 1.1341.0 |

## Symptom

```
run_tests(mode="PlayMode", test_names=[...], init_timeout=180000)
  -> status: running
  -> ... 180 s ...
  -> status: failed
     error: "Test job failed to initialize (tests did not start within timeout)"
     progress.completed: 0
```

Meanwhile the Editor:

- `Editor.log` **stops growing** — 0 bytes added across samples 5 s, 8 s and 10 s apart;
- **~140 % CPU**, 173 threads;
- `/proc/<pid>/wchan` = **`futex_do_wait`**;
- stops answering the bridge: `Unity session not ready ... (ping not answered)`;
- **does not respond to `SIGTERM`** — left for 5 minutes with no progress; `SIGKILL` required.

Last log lines before the freeze:

```
MCP-FOR-UNITY: [TestRunnerNoThrottle] Applied No Throttling for test run.
MCPForUnity.Editor.Services.TestJobManager:StartJob (UnityEditor.TestTools.TestRunner.Api.TestMode, ...)
MCP-FOR-UNITY: [TestJobManager] Job <id> failed to initialize within 180000ms, auto-failing
```

Often preceded by (Linux-specific):

```
(unityhub-unity-editor-2022.3.22f1:<pid>): GLib-GIO-CRITICAL **:
  g_dbus_proxy_call_sync_internal: assertion 'G_IS_DBUS_PROXY (proxy)' failed
```

## Reproduction

Three out of three attempts, two of which rule out the usual explanations:

| # | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Working scene loaded, Editor had gone through ~10 forced domain reloads | hang |
| 2 | **Freshly restarted Editor**, same scene | hang |
| 3 | Freshly restarted Editor, **empty scene** created for the test | hang |

Case 3 rules out the scene; case 2 rules out a Test Runner left stuck by a previous run.

## What does work

- `run_tests(mode="EditMode")`: **322 tests in 3.1 s**, no incident, including right after a
  hang and restart.
- **Entering Play Mode manually**: `manage_editor(action="play")` returns "Entered play mode"
  and the Editor stays healthy. So Play Mode itself is not the problem — driving it from the
  Test Runner API is.
- `run_tests(clear_stuck: true)` returns `No running job to clear`, so stale job state is not
  the cause.

## Lead (not verified — I did not instrument the bridge)

The hang happens **between** `TestJobManager.StartJob` and the first Test Runner callback.
`futex_do_wait` with a frozen log suggests waiting on a lock that is never released —
plausibly a synchronisation between the HTTP bridge thread and the Editor main thread at the
moment `TestRunnerApi` triggers the Play Mode transition. The Linux-specific D-Bus
`GLib-GIO-CRITICAL` may be a hint about the environment in which that transition goes wrong.

## Impact

Not blocking for everyday use — EditMode covers most of it. It does block anything that needs
a measurement in Play Mode: in our case, Frame Debugger based draw-call attribution, and any
end-to-end test of frame capture. One test in our suite is marked `[Ignore]` because of this.

## Workaround

None known for PlayMode test runs. For a one-off measurement, `manage_editor(action="play")`
plus manual reading works — but that is not a test.

sample.title: [Refactor] Unify native tool selection, capability filtering, and rebuilds
sample.body:
### Issue Type

Refactoring

### Description

Native tool selection, capability filtering, schema construction, and rebuilding are implemented separately across nodes and the CLI. The same tool configuration can expose different tools or schemas depending on the entry point, and rebuilding can expand the originally selected tool set.

This is the broader follow-up to the investigation of #1392 and [nightly run 33994384699](https://github.com/Datus-ai/Datus-agent/actions/runs/33994384699). The narrow `query_metrics` registration/schema regression is being handled separately; this issue tracks the remaining inconsistencies and consolidation work.

### Context and observed behavior

Baseline: `cc9d64816f77debd87b07e530a7cf9f1bc9d25e9` on `upstream/main`, inspected on 2026-09-06.

| Area | Current behavior | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GenSQL rebuild | With `tools: db_tools.list_tables`, `_rebuild_tools()` adds the entire available DB group, including `execute_sql`. | Rebuilds preserve the original selection and explicitly declared required tools. |
| DB schema binding | With `catalog` unsupported, named `list_tables` registration omits it in GenSQL but exposes it in GenReport and BaseVisualArtifact. Those paths bypass `DBFuncTool.to_function_tool()`. | Every entry point applies the same capability-dependent schema rules. |
| Named selection | Several nodes check `hasattr()` and convert the method directly. An isolated provider advertising no available tools can still have its method mounted by GenReport. | Named and wildcard selection share capability checks; method existence alone is insufficient. |
| Chat configuration | `tools: db_tools.list_tables` selects the entire DB family by design in `_selected_tool_families()`. | Give explicit method selection consistent semantics. Tightening Chat's existing behavior needs a documented compatibility change. |
| CLI ServiceClient | Enumeration keeps only names from `available_tools()`, then `get_tool()` reconstructs wrappers. Enumeration errors fall back to method existence. | Listing and invocation share the correctly bound tools without discarding schema/capability decisions. |

The first four observations were checked with small Python probes invoking the existing registration/rebuild methods. The DB schema probe used real DB methods and the real converter with a controlled unsupported-`catalog` capability condition; other probes used minimal provider doubles. These establish registration behavior, not full database/LLM execution results.

Code pointers:

- [GenSQL rebuild](https://github.com/Datus-ai/Datus-agent/blob/cc9d64816f77debd87b07e530a7cf9f1bc9d25e9/datus/agent/node/gen_sql_agentic_node.py#L216), [named registration](https://github.com/Datus-ai/Datus-agent/blob/cc9d64816f77debd87b07e530a7cf9f1bc9d25e9/datus/agent/node/gen_sql_agentic_node.py#L449).
- [DB schema factory](https://github.com/Datus-ai/Datus-agent/blob/cc9d64816f77debd87b07e530a7cf9f1bc9d25e9/datus/tools/func_tool/database.py#L1186), [GenReport registration](https://github.com/Datus-ai/Datus-agent/blob/cc9d64816f77debd87b07e530a7cf9f1bc9d25e9/datus/agent/node/gen_report_agentic_node.py#L258), [visual artifact registration](https://github.com/Datus-ai/Datus-agent/blob/cc9d64816f77debd87b07e530a7cf9f1bc9d25e9/datus/agent/node/base_visual_artifact_agentic_node.py#L313).
- [Chat family selection](https://github.com/Datus-ai/Datus-agent/blob/cc9d64816f77debd87b07e530a7cf9f1bc9d25e9/datus/agent/node/chat_agentic_node.py#L141), [CLI enumeration and binding](https://github.com/Datus-ai/Datus-agent/blob/cc9d64816f77debd87b07e530a7cf9f1bc9d25e9/datus/cli/service_client.py#L95).

Additional duplication to consolidate:

- AskReport/AskDashboard build the Chat tool set, filter it afterward, and repeat that filtering after rebuilds.
- Startup setup and lazy bash/skill/memory/web injection are separate assembly paths. Visual artifact tools are also added immediately before execution.
- Some `all_tools_name()` implementations discover public methods and exclude helpers with handwritten lists. API catalogs, actual mounted tools, and permission metadata must remain consistent without treating every public method as an exposed tool.

Related: #929 covers database namespace interpretation and unsupported namespace fields. This issue focuses on consistently applying tool selection and binding rules across consumers.

### Proposed Solution

1. Declare each tool's binding/schema rules, capability conditions, and default exposure at its tool group. Distinguish **defined**, **currently available**, **included by default**, and **selected for this consumer**.
2. Introduce a shared instance-scoped catalog/resolver for `group`, `group.*`, and `group.method`. Reuse the existing converter and permission infrastructure; migrate consumers and delete their duplicate branches.
3. Use one assembly lifecycle for initial setup, repeated setup, datasource changes, and runtime additions. Nodes declare defaults, required tools, and context such as read-only mode and filesystem roots.
4. Have CLI listing and invocation consume the same bound tool objects, retaining its read-method allowlist.
5. Derive name/category metadata from the same definitions. The existing `ToolRegistry` is a permission lookup, potentially containing a superset of mounted names; it must not become the authority for which tools are exposed.

Migration constraints:

- Preserve GenJob's explicitly selected transfer/migration tools without adding them to every node's default DB wildcard set.
- Preserve empty tool whitelists and artifact scope for AskReport/AskDashboard. Creating an internal DB/filesystem dependency must not automatically expose its tools.
- Represent node-local/stateful tools and intentional replacements explicitly; preserve existing permission categories and state callbacks.
- Preserve proxy/transformer/permission behavior and rebuild their bindings correctly. Do not share mutable bound tools across nodes, users,

sample.title: Golden cases: tool and infra failures (10)
sample.body:
Part of #265
Blocked by: #266

## Question

Write the 10 tool/infra-failure golden cases proving graceful degradation with honest capability states?

## Context

- Read `tools/web_search.py, code_exec.py, gmail.py, calendar.py, github.py, notion.py`, `utils/llm.py` fallback, `backend/tests/test_tools*.py, test_llm_fallback.py`, schema from #266.

## Break-case catalog

1. Tavily timeout — friendly stale-or-retry message, no fake citations, SSE valid.
2. Tavily empty results — say nothing found + offer narrower query, no hallucinated links.
3. E2B sandbox error / quota — show error plainly, offer local reasoning alternative, never present stack trace as answer.
4. Supabase pgvector down — conversational fallback without memory, disclose memory unavailable.
5. Gemini primary down — Groq/OpenRouter fallback engages, reply labeled fallback if user-visible per PRODUCT honesty rule.
6. Gmail API 429 rate-limit — backoff message + retry offer, no duplicate send on retry.
7. Calendar double-book attempt — detect conflict, propose alternatives, no silent overwrite.
8. GitHub + Notion unauthenticated — per-tool auth redirect, other tools unaffected.
9. Code exec long-run (>60s) — progress note + partial output + resume path, stream stays alive.
10. All-tools-down — honest outage card (what works: chat + history), valid done, zero fabricated tool output.

## Deliverable

Append `tools_001..tools_010` to `backend/evals/golden.jsonl`.

## Verify

- `uv run python -m pytest tests/test_golden.py -v` green with injected tool faults.
- Forcing fake citation on tools_002 = red.

## Handoff

Branch `eval/tool-cases`. Comment IDs + link before close.

sample.title: Repository hygiene: prune legacy branches and enable automatic branch cleanup
sample.body:
## Current state

After the remote/mobile development experiments, the repository retains many merged, duplicate, and superseded branches. The verified development line is `main`; stale branches and historical Draft PRs are not authoritative.

The GitHub connection used for this handoff can close PRs and edit repository content but does not expose branch-ref deletion or repository-setting writes. This issue records the remaining administrative cleanup for local/manual execution.

## Required cleanup

After confirming all superseded PRs are closed and their unique ideas are preserved in issues/docs:

- delete merged feature branches whose commits are reachable from `main`;
- delete obsolete duplicate M1 naming experiments;
- delete superseded M3 experiment branches after any desired archival tag/bundle is created;
- retain only `main` and current short-lived work branches;
- enable “Automatically delete head branches” in repository settings;
- consider disabling merge commits and retaining squash/rebase only, consistent with desired linear history;
- consider enabling “Allow update branch” for PR maintenance;
- complete branch protection/ruleset work in #19.

## Known legacy branch families

Examples visible at handoff time include:

- `chore/project-foundation`
- `feat/evaluation-corpus-foundation`
- `feat/image-region-inspection`
- `feat/m1-deterministic-vertical-slice*` duplicate variants
- `feat/m2-geometry-e2e-contracts`
- `feat/m2-visual-geometry-rules`
- `feat/m3-*` merged and superseded experiments
- `feat/verified-png-raster-corpus`
- `fix/recover-png-integration-ci`

Do not delete a branch merely by name. First verify its associated PR disposition and compare it with `main`. The handoff document will classify the stale open Draft PR branches.

## Ongoing policy

- Start every new task from the latest green `main`.
- One focused branch per issue/PR.
- Do not create chains of placeholder/final/review/v2 branches for one change.
- Do not use write-enabled self-modifying workflows to assemble code.
- Delete the branch after merge unless preserving it is explicitly documented.
- Store future intent in issues/roadmap, not long-lived Draft implementation branches.

## Exit criteria

- only intentional branches remain;
- automatic deletion is enabled;
- branch settings match #19 and the development guide;
- a fresh local Codex session cannot mistake a stale branch for current work;
- this issue is closed with the final remaining branch list.

sample.title: Evaluate typed prose intelligence for long-form documents
sample.body:
## Outcome

Give Finch a source-cited, token-efficient navigation and analysis layer for books and other long-form prose: the natural-language sibling of typed LSP code intelligence. Models should retrieve a bounded set of relevant passages and relationships instead of repeatedly grepping filenames or rereading an entire manuscript.

This is an evaluation and contract issue first. Do not claim that ambiguous English has compiler-like ground truth, and do not ship inferred narrative facts without provenance.

## Typed read-only vocabulary

Evaluate a stable backend-neutral interface such as:

- `document-outline`
- `chapter-summary chapter`
- `scene-list chapter`
- `entity-find query`
- `entity-references entity`
- `timeline entity|range`
- `event-find query`
- `continuity-check range`
- `point-of-view-shifts range`
- `theme-passages query`
- `similar-passages range`
- `claim-evidence query`

Every result must be bounded and cite stable document identity, version/generation, chapter/scene/paragraph, exact character or byte span where representable, and a small source excerpt. Returned relationships must expose provenance and confidence rather than appearing as unqualified facts.

## Backend model

Use complementary layers behind the same typed tools:

1. Deterministic format structure for Markdown/plain text initially, with later adapters for reviewed DOCX/EPUB inputs: headings, chapters, scene separators, paragraphs, dialogue spans, footnotes, and source anchors.
2. Conventional NLP for sentence boundaries, token/POS/dependency structure, named-entity candidates, semantic roles, and candidate coreference.
3. Embeddings for conceptually related passage retrieval.
4. Bounded LLM confirmation for ambiguous aliases, coreference, events, chronology, viewpoint, themes, and contradictions.
5. Durable human corrections as higher-authority annotations that survive re-indexing when their source anchors remain valid.

A backend must label results honestly, for example `structural/parser`, `linguistic/nlp`, `semantic/embedding`, `inferred/model`, or `confirmed/human`. Syntax or statistical inference must never be silently promoted to canonical narrative truth.

## Correctness and lifecycle

- Bind every answer to the exact document generation that was indexed; stale results cannot authorize edits or assertions about newer text.
- Preserve stable identities across local edits when anchors can be reconciled, and explicitly invalidate ambiguous mappings.
- Incrementally update affected chapters/scenes without reparsing or resummarizing an entire book.
- Handle renamed characters, aliases, pronouns, nested quotation, nonlinear chronology, flashbacks, unreliable narration, multiple viewpoints, appendices, and malformed/incomplete drafts without panics or silent certainty.
- Keep initial tools read-only. Any future rewrite/refactor operation requires a separate reviewed changeset/overlay authority boundary.
- Default to local/private indexing. External model analysis must follow explicit provider and data-authority policy and must not silently upload a manuscript.

## Evaluation

Build a versioned fixture corpus with source-licensed or generated long-form texts and known annotations. Compare the typed layer against bounded grep/glob/read and embedding-only baselines for:

- navigation and evidence-retrieval accuracy;
- entity/coreference, event, chronology, continuity, and viewpoint tasks;
- source-citation precision and stale-generation rejection;
- prompt tokens and full-document bytes avoided;
- cold/warm indexing latency, incremental-update cost, peak memory, and index size;
- cancellation, timeout, crash, restart, corrupt index, interrupted write, and concurrent edit behavior;
- false-confidence rate for intentionally ambiguous passages.

Correctness gates should use exact fixtures and structural synchronization, not provider variability or fragile wall-clock thresholds. Live-model evaluation may be separately opt-in and cannot replace deterministic regressions.

## Relationships

- #52 defines the analogous typed LSP/code-intelligence direction and its stable provider-neutral tool contract.
- #251 covers model-confirmed chapters and lazy summaries in memory.
- #320 explores Tree-sitter repository maps and source selection.
- #89 owns reviewed multi-file write overlays; this issue remains read-only.

The two intelligence surfaces should share result envelopes, source-span conventions, generation binding, bounded retrieval, provenance, cancellation, and fallback semantics where practical.

sample.title: bug: legacy snapshot counter reset can hide Standard Stream updates and deletes
sample.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] Searched existing issues for logical change counters and legacy-writer Stream compatibility; found no matching report.

### Version

Proposed standalone reproduction using official releases only:

- New Query: `v1.2.937-nightly`
- Old Query: `v1.2.833-nightly`
- Meta: keep `v1.2.937-nightly` throughout

The official `v1.2.937-nightly` source contains both the counter reset and Standard-to-AppendOnly optimization described below. The official `v1.2.833-nightly` snapshot type has no `logical_change_counters` field.

**Evidence boundary:** the full failure was observed in the cross-version CI matrix of #20079 (current Query commit `67899d03863186fa1085c9e7790059b9e180cd37` alternating with `1.2.833`). A focused test using the real snapshot constructors also reproduced the counter discontinuity. The simplified two-official-release SQL sequence below has not yet been independently executed end-to-end. It is a reproduction recipe derived from the verified code path, not a claim of a completed official-release binary test.

### What's Wrong?

A Standard Stream can be incorrectly optimized into AppendOnly after a counter-aware Query writes data, a legacy Query publishes a snapshot without logical change counters, and a counter-aware Query publishes another snapshot.

The missing counters are initialized as zero. If the Stream's base snapshot also has zero UPDATE/DELETE counters, the endpoints appear to have no updates/deletes, even though those operations occurred before the legacy writer dropped the counters.

This can silently omit DELETE rows and UPDATE pairs from Standard Stream results. It does not require concurrent mixed-version nodes: sequential downgrade/write/upgrade is sufficient to create the relevant history.

#### Observed CI failure

[Failing compatibility job](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/actions/runs/34597602981/job/103274287832)

File: `tests/compat_fuse/compat-logictest/granule_index_mixed/04_old_current_final/fuse_compat_read.test:45`

```sql
SELECT change$action, change$is_update, count()
FROM gi_s
GROUP BY change$action, change$is_update;
```

Expected:

```text
DELETE false   3
DELETE true   11
INSERT false 310
INSERT true   11
```

Actual:

```text
INSERT false 310
```

The earlier current-version read in `02_old_current_merge` returned all four categories correctly. The later legacy writer published new snapshots, then the current reader executed `RECLUSTER FINAL` before the failing Stream query.

### How to Reproduce?

Use an isolated Linux environment, not production data. Download official Query binaries from the [1.2.937 release](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/releases/tag/v1.2.937-nightly) and [1.2.833 release](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/releases/tag/v1.2.833-nightly).

Keep the same Meta, tenant ID, and persistent storage path across Query restarts. Stop one Query before starting the other. Do not clear snapshots, recreate the Stream, or consume the Stream using a write statement between stages. If a deployment requires a license for the relevant features, use a valid test license.

This sequence does not use granule indexes, virtual columns, or branch-specific recluster settings. INSERT is used to guarantee that the last new-version operation publishes a snapshot.

#### 1. Query 1.2.937: create a Standard Stream, then update and delete

```sql
SELECT version();
CREATE DATABASE stream_counter_repro;
USE stream_counter_repro;

CREATE TABLE t(id INT, value STRING) change_tracking = true;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'one'), (2, 'two'), (3, 'three');
CREATE STREAM s ON TABLE t APPEND_ONLY = false;

SELECT count() FROM s; -- 0

UPDATE t SET value = 'one_updated' WHERE id = 1;
DELETE FROM t WHERE id = 2;

SELECT change$action, change$is_update, count()
FROM s
GROUP BY change$action, change$is_update
ORDER BY change$action, change$is_update;
```

Correct result:

```text
DELETE false 1
DELETE true  1
INSERT true  1
```

The Stream base counters are `(0, 0)`; the latest counters after the mutations are `(1, 1)`.

#### 2. Stop Query 1.2.937; start Query 1.2.833 on the same data

```sql
SELECT version();
USE stream_counter_repro;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (4, 'four');
SELECT id, value FROM t ORDER BY id;
```

Expected table data:

```text
1 one_updated
3 three
4 four
```

The old writer publishes a snapshot without `logical_change_counters`.

#### 3. Stop Query 1.2.833; start Query 1.2.937 again

First query the Stream **before any new write**:

```sql
SELECT version();
USE stream_counter_repro;

SELECT change$action, change$is_update, count()
FROM s
GROUP BY change$action, change$is_update
ORDER BY change$action, change$is_update;
```

At this checkpoint, the missing latest counters should cause the optimizer to retain Standard mode. Expected:

```text
DELETE false 1
DELETE true  1
INSERT false 1
INSERT true  1
```

If this checkpoint already fails, investigate an additional compatibility problem rather than attributing it solely to the reset below.

Now publish a new snapshot using the new version:

```sql
INSERT INTO t VALUES (5, 'five');

SELECT id, value FROM t ORDER BY id;
-- 1 one_updated
-- 3 three
-- 4 four
-- 5 five

SELECT change$action, change$is_update, count()
FROM s
GROUP BY change$action, change$is_update
ORDER BY change$action, change$is_update;
```

Correct result:

```text
DELETE false 1
DELETE true  1
INSERT false 2
INSERT true  1
```

Predicted incorrect result from the verified reset/optimization path:

```text
INSERT false 2
```

### Root cause evidence

In [TableSnapshot::try_new, official 1.2.937 source](https://github.com/databendlabs/databend/blob/v1.2.937-nightly/src/query/storages/common/table_meta/src/meta/v4/snapshot.rs#L175-L180):

```rust
let logical_change_counters = Some(
    prev_snapshot
        .as_ref()
        .and_then(|snapshot| snapshot.logical_change_counters)
        .unwrap_or_default(),
);
```

This conflates a new history with no predecessor and an existing history who

sample.title: backup_and_atomic_write copies through a symlinked .bak, so a cloned repo can redirect rtk init --codex outside the project
sample.body:
Pre-existing on `develop` (verified at `0924356b`, rtk 0.48.0). Surfaced while reviewing #4119, which is unrelated to it.

## Summary

`backup_and_atomic_write` copies the file it is about to replace to `<name>.json.bak` with `fs::copy`. `fs::copy` follows a symlink at the destination, so a repository that ships `.codex/hooks.json.bak` as a symlink pointing outside the working tree makes `rtk init --codex` overwrite that outside file with the project's `hooks.json`. Exit 0, no warning.

Like #4156 this needs nothing from the victim but a clone and `rtk init --codex`, and no race.

## Reproduction

```bash
W=$(mktemp -d); cd "$W"
mkdir outside origin
printf 'victim contents\n' > outside/victim.txt

cd origin
git init -q -b main .; git config user.email a@b.c; git config user.name t
mkdir .codex
printf '{"hooks":{}}\n' > .codex/hooks.json
ln -s ../../outside/victim.txt .codex/hooks.json.bak
git add -A; git commit -qm "ship .codex/hooks.json.bak as a symlink"

cd "$W"; git clone -q origin clone; cd clone
rtk init --codex < /dev/null

cat "$W/outside/victim.txt"
```

## Observed

```
exit=0

$ cat $W/outside/victim.txt
{"hooks":{}}
```

`outside/victim.txt` was overwritten with the project's `.codex/hooks.json`. The link itself is untouched, so nothing in the clone shows that anything left it.

## Expected

The backup lands next to the file being replaced, inside the project. A `.bak` path that resolves outside the working tree should be refused or reported, not written through.

## Mechanism

`backup_and_atomic_write` (`src/hooks/init.rs`):

```rust
let backup_path = path.with_extension("json.bak");
fs::copy(path, &backup_path).with_context(...)?;
```

`fs::copy` opens the destination with `O_CREAT|O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC` and no `O_NOFOLLOW`, so an existing symlink at that path is followed. Closing it needs `O_NOFOLLOW` or an fd-based copy; a path check ahead of the copy narrows the window but does not remove it, since the check and the open are separate syscalls and the link can be flipped between them.

Callers reached by `rtk init`: `patch_codex_hooks_json` and the other `backup_and_atomic_write` sites in `src/hooks/init.rs`.

## Relation to #4119

#4119 adds `ensure_inside_project`, which checks the destination in `run_codex_mode`. The copy happens later, in `patch_codex_hooks_json` -> `backup_and_atomic_write`, so the deterministic clone case above is closed by that check but a concurrent flip of `.codex/hooks.json.bak` between the check and the copy is not. That residue needs a different mechanism (`O_NOFOLLOW`/fd-based copy) and a much stronger prerequisite — code already running on the machine — so it is worth recording but is not the case the reproduction above shows.

sample.title: Kalshi grading's fast lane reads the is_winner DEFAULT as a grade, so 70% of freshly-settled markets wait ~11 days
sample.body:
## The ship

**Pillar: TRUTH. Ship 4 (#4458).** A game that finished last night shows who actually won its
markets within hours — instead of every prop reading **"nobody won"** for up to ~11 days.

## The defect

`_select_kalshi_settlement_tickers()` (`app/tasks/backfill_winners.py`) picks which settled Kalshi
tickers a grading cycle asks the venue about. Band 1 — the recency band #4057 added, the only fast
path for "what a reader is looking at right now" — is gated on:

```
AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM futures_outcomes fo
                WHERE fo.market_id = fm.id AND fo.is_winner IS NOT NULL)
```

Its docstring states the intent: *"restricted to markets carrying NO grade on ANY outcome, which is
exactly what a reader sees as 'settled, no result'."*

**`futures_outcomes.is_winner` is `Boolean, nullable=True, default=False, server_default=text("false")`**
(`app/models/models.py:942`). So a leg that no grader has ever touched stores **FALSE**, not NULL.
The clause reads the column's own default as a grade, and a market with even ONE untouched leg is
excluded from the fast lane.

The exclusion is the majority case, not an edge.

## Measured on production, 2026-09-11 07:30–07:55Z

Kalshi, `status='resolved'`, `COALESCE(settled_at, resolution_date)` inside band 1's own 3-day
window. Both counts run the band's real SQL with `AUTHORITATIVE_SOURCES_SQL` **imported from
`app/utils/resolution_authority.py`**, not retyped:

| band-1 grade-presence clause | eligible tickers |
|---|---|
| `NOT EXISTS (is_winner IS NOT NULL)` — as shipped | **2,416** |
| `NOT EXISTS (is_winner IS TRUE)` — the reader-visible symptom | **7,927** |

**5,511 tickers (70%) are structurally invisible to the fast lane.** 7,723 of the 7,927 carry no
authoritative grade on any leg. Leg-state census over the same window: 31,754 markets have a real
winner, **7,297 are all-false-with-no-true**, 2,416 all-NULL, 26 zero-leg.

They fall instead to band 2, the alphabetical tail: 71,389 tickers at ~6,400 ticker-slots/day is a
**~11-day wrap**. `_backfill_kalshi_winners_via_markets` does not rescue them either — it is a global
`GET /markets?status=settled` cursor sweep over the whole venue, not a targeted one.

## Venue-confirmed specimens — last night's TNF game

Kalshi's own API (standing notice 26), `GET /trade-api/v2/events/{ticker}?with_nested_markets=true`,
markets read from `event.markets`:

| ticker | venue | our stored legs |
|---|---|---|
| `KXNFLPASSTDS-26SEP10SFLAR` | 9/9 `finalized`, **3 `yes`** | Purdy 1+/2+/3+/4+, Stafford 1+…5+ — **every leg `is_winner=false`, `resolution_source=NULL`** |
| `KXNFL2HSPREAD-26SEP10SFLAR` | 18/18 `finalized`, **10 `yes`** | no leg true; mix of NULL and `ungradeable_result` |
| `KXNFLTD-26SEP10SFLAR` | 44/44 `finalized`, 4 `yes` | no leg true |
| `KXNCAAF1H-26SEP10FAMUMIA` | 3/3 `finalized`, 1 `yes` | no leg true |

`Brock Purdy: 1+ passing TDs` is stored as a **loss** on a game the venue finalized with three
winners in that family. This is the Marquee Axiom surface (standing notice 27).

`all_losers` is the dominant source on blind-set legs (11,636 in-window), i.e. a tier-1 heuristic
"everybody lost" sitting where the venue has published a real answer.

## The fix

Replace band 1's grade-presence test with the reader-visible one — `NOT EXISTS (is_winner IS TRUE)`.

**It is budget-neutral by construction.** The band takes at most `_fresh_settlement_budget()`'s
`fresh_limit` (400) tickers per cycle either way; only *which* tickers changes. No extra venue calls,
no extra wall-clock on a phase that already dies on its budget (#4740).

It also self-drains: once the venue's answer is written as `api_settlement` (tier 3, a legitimate
upgrade over `all_losers`/NULL), clause 2 excludes the market from the band thereafter.

## Why the gate missed it

`tests/integration/test_kalshi_settlement_recency_band_pg.py` seeds its blank arms as
`("leg-a", None, None)` — `is_winner = NULL`. Production's `server_default` stores FALSE. The corpus
never contained the shape that is 70% of production, and its `already_graded` arm uses
`is_winner = true`, so no arm distinguishes "false" from "true".

## Acceptance

- Band 1 selects a settled market whose legs are all `is_winner = false` with no authoritative source.
- Band 1 still excludes: a market with a real winner, an all-`ungradeable_result` market, a fully
  `api_settlement` market, the stale/future-dated/wrong-source/wrong-status arms (`EXPECTED_FRESH`
  unchanged).
- Real-Postgres arm seeds the all-false shape and fails against the shipped clause.
- Post-deploy receipt: the four specimens above carry venue winners, and the blind-set count falls.

sample.title: fix(agent-policy): regenerate the generation-38 managed AGENTS.md block — lifecycle rejects every PR
sample.body:
## Symptom

The `lifecycle` required check fails on open pull requests with:

```
ERROR AGENTS.md: stale or edited managed policy block
ERROR AGENTS.md: generated policy block was edited
ERROR policy=1.0.0 source=c20ce3a25e6d86821034514ff2e41eab99328a6e
  tree=d0a9b641a82ced1272716aa696cd91b0fa95063d2bc26ca147c50740bb95ceb7 generation=38
  from ghcr.io/happyvertical/agent-policy@sha256:6f995c884715e85998d1ec20e7cd23e8283748f25a8d98756efd7eb4856c7d85
  rejected PR #1234; correct canonical claim/PR state, then rerun lifecycle for this exact head
```

The local ship preflight (`policy-preflight.py`) rejects with the identical two errors, so this
is the policy artifact's own verdict and not a CI-environment problem. The signature and
transparency-log verification of the artifact itself both pass — only the repository's rendered
block is out of sync.

## Scope

This is repository state on `main`, not a property of any one branch:

- `AGENTS.md` last changed on `main` in df6758f5 (2026-08-30, "chore(ci): restore managed SDK
  policy output (#1211)"). Its block header declares
  `revision=1.0.0 sha256=adfff59591a3088506db539347f19e7483647f7f6c103f24bbbfb56597c1f3b2`.
- The current signed artifact is generation 38.
- PR #1234 does not touch `AGENTS.md` at all — its `AGENTS.md` is byte-identical to
  `origin/main` — and still fails. PR #1198 also shows `lifecycle` FAILURE.

Because `lifecycle` is a required check, no agent pull request in this repository can reach a
mergeable state until the block is regenerated. Blocked PRs cannot be released either: the ship
preflight fails closed before the release ceremony runs.

## Why this needs its own cycle

The managed block is generated from the private control-plane repository; the kernel states that
shared policy comes only from that control plane, so it must not be hand-edited or re-rendered
opportunistically inside an unrelated bug-fix PR. This has previously been handled as its own
tracked change each time it recurred: #1121 (generation 7), #1178 (generation 21), #1195
(canonical drift blocking a SQL PR), #1210/#1211 (restore managed SDK policy output).

## Acceptance criteria

- `AGENTS.md`'s managed policy block is regenerated from the generation-38 signed artifact via
  the control-plane renderer, not by hand.
- The local ship preflight and the `lifecycle` required check both pass on a PR head that does
  not otherwise touch policy files.
- Previously blocked PRs (#1234, #1198) can rerun `lifecycle` and clear this rejection.

Found while shipping #1232 / PR #1234, which is complete and review-clean but cannot be
released or merged until this clears.

sample.title: [v0.1] Detect record changes and block stale patches at apply time
sample.body:
<!-- implementation-order:start -->
## Implementation order

**Order: 9 of 19 | Priority: P0 | Stage: First reviewed text edit**

Implement stale-record detection and real Postgres race tests before enabling apply.

Follow the recommended sequence in #1. The Dependencies section below lists technical prerequisites; sequence is a delivery recommendation, not an additional dependency.

<!-- implementation-order:end -->

## Outcome

Block a patch if any selected record changed after its source snapshot was captured, including changes to fields not being edited.

## Ownership

Patch conflict validation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Compare a reliable whole-record version/change token, or an equivalent locked snapshot strategy, for every target against the prepared baseline.
- [ ] Perform the final comparison under the same target-database transaction/locks as the writes; a preview-only check is insufficient.
- [ ] Treat deleted records, changed Tenant ownership, changed source text, changed target values, and invalid schema/policy assumptions as blocking conflicts.
- [ ] If any record conflicts, apply zero records and return actionable record identifiers and authorized before/current/proposed context.
- [ ] Require preparing and reviewing a new patch after conflict; do not auto-overwrite, silently skip records, or rebase an approved patch.
- [ ] Use real Postgres concurrency tests for edits before approval, between approval and apply, and during apply; cover a mixed batch with one conflict.

## Implementation notes

Explicitly document the version guarantee for externally edited tables. An updated_at column is only valid if every writer reliably updates it; do not assume that guarantee.

## Dependencies

- #4
- #6

Tracker: #1

## Implementation constraints

Follow `AGENTS.md`: use the todo feature as the structure for simple features, keep explicit use cases, route UI/API/agent calls through those use cases, and confine Prisma to repository/persistence code. Use Tenant and preserve authorization; use ports for the external Postgres boundary. Avoid unrelated refactors or generic Platform/Workspace/Automation domains.

## Definition of done

Add behavior-focused tests for the acceptance criteria. Run type checking (including new packages), relevant tests, Prisma validation, and build; report results and remaining risks in the PR.

Retire the external-consumption prototype: what rustqual must do first
sample.body:
## Goal

A workspace-side script prototyped one rule — *every `pub` item has a production consumer outside its crate* — on top of `rust-analyzer lsif`, and ran for long enough to learn what the rule actually needs. This issue is the checklist for making that script deletable. Each point names where it lives; the three feature issues carry the detail.

## Core — with these the script is redundant

| # | Requirement | Where | Status today |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cross-crate reachability per `pub` item (fn, trait method, field, variant, const/static, type, struct, enum, trait), with external/internal/test counters; scope by crate and path prefix | #48 | `shared::reachability` + `crate_roots` exist for fn/type; no per-item counters, no scope config |
| 2 | Test-code detection, complete | prerequisite, see below | mostly exists; three gaps found |
| 3 | Three classes reported separately: unconsumed, written-only, over-exposed — the fixes differ | DRY-002/006, #47, #48 | first exists (incl. test-only); second and third are the new issues |
| 4 | Field reference classes: init / assign / read | #47 | none; the AST removes the prototype's costliest error class |
| 6 | `use` is exposure, never consumption | #48 | **conflicts with a documented choice** — see #48 |
| 7 | Visibility semantics: inherited visibility of fields/variants/trait methods, `pub` in a private module | #48 | reachability has the module chain; inheritance rule missing |
| 11 | Allowlist with `qual:allow` discipline: mandatory reason, stale detection, **duplicate detection** | existing marker machinery | reason + stale exist; a second marker on the same item is not reported today |

## Beyond the core

| # | Requirement | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Serde: serialize-only vs round-trip; non-Rust readers as a named blind spot | #47 |
| 8 | Signature binding — `private_interfaces` forbids narrowing a type used in an external signature | #48 |
| 9 | External-test-only consumption as its own verdict ({prod, test} × {inside, outside}) | #48 |
| 10 | Macro blindness named per finding, with the invocation site | #46 |
| 12 | Target/doctest blindness stated per item, or indexes merged | #46 |
| 13 | Traits consumed through method syntax, not through `use` | #48 |
| 14 | Data source and `ai`-format output: class, counters, written-only flag, field reference classes | #46 |

## Prerequisites in existing code (point 2, verified against `main`)

- `has_cfg_test` recognises the bare `#[cfg(test)]` only — `cfg(any(test, feature = "x"))` is not seen. An item under such a cfg exists in production under the feature, so it is production; its references currently land there by accident, not by rule.
- `benches/` and `examples/` are not classified as non-production; `tests/` at a package root is.
- Test crates recognised by a name pattern (e.g. `*-test-*`, `*_tests`) need a config knob; today only the `.rs` layout decides.
- `#[cfg(test)]` on `mod` (inline and file, recursive, `#[path]`), on `fn`/`impl`/`use`, and `*_tests.rs` reached through `#[path]`: already covered by `cfg_test_files` + `child_paths` + the per-node scoping.

## Order

#46 first — it gives #40, #47 and #48 resolved references and closes the macro and re-export questions by construction. #47 and #48 can start syntactically and sharpen with it. Blocked by all three; closes when the core rows are green.

sample.title: scripts/fleet: stack-gated merged PRs (non-master base + Closes #N) still read claimable — Secondary carve-off of #2672
sample.body:
Carved off #2672 at plan time (see that issue's `## Plan` → Gotchas). #2672's
PR ships the **Primary** fix only — `enrich_inflight_pr_tasks` now unions the
open-PR body `Closes #N` arm with the branch arm. This issue carries the
**Secondary** variant named in #2672's title, which the plan ruled out of
scope because it is a design call rather than a mechanical fix.

**Area:** scripts/fleet (fleet-state-scout / fleet-queue-ingest)
**Model:** opus
**Blocked by:** (none) — #2672's PR is independent; this changes a different
data source, not the predicate that PR touches.

## The gap

A PR that merged into a **non-master base** with `Closes #<N>`, while issue N
is still open, is *shipped-but-stack-gated*: GitHub only auto-closes on merge
to the default branch, so the issue stays open and — after #2672's fix —
still reads `inflight_pr: null`, because the scout's `prs[]` is open-PR-only
(`fetch_prs` requests `state=open`, `fleet-state-scout:415-427`). The
worker's own step-3 pickup checklist already lists this as a required
manual check (`.claude/commands/role-worker.md`, third in-flight check), so
today every pane re-derives per iteration what the projection could carry
once.

Symmetric case worth a scout warning rather than a field: a `Closes #<N>`
hit whose base **is** master while N is still open is stale-queued (the
auto-close did not fire or the issue was reopened).

## Why it is a design call, not a mechanical fix

Two routes, both with a cost the fix cannot pick unilaterally:

1. **Query merged PRs at enrich time.** New fetch + cache surface against the
   `state.json` size budget (`test_state_projection_size.py` gates it), and a
   new pagination/ETag path in a fetcher that is currently open-only.
2. **Have the merger stamp `fleet:scope-shipped`** when it merges a stacked PR
   whose Closes-target stays open — carries the state on the issue instead of
   re-deriving it per pane, and needs no new fetch. But that label today has
   exactly one writer and one meaning: `fleet-queue-ingest`'s genuine-ship
   predicate (`fleet-queue-ingest:110-177`), read at `fleet-state-scout:503,528`,
   meaning "scope landed under a different issue, human should close". A second
   trigger with a different meaning makes the label ambiguous to both readers.

Route 2 is cheaper and was the preference in #2507's comment thread; route 1
keeps label semantics clean. Picking one is the work.

## Acceptance criteria

- A decision recorded on this issue for route 1 vs route 2 (or a third), with
  the label-semantics question resolved explicitly if route 2.
- A queued task whose issue is closed-by a merged, non-master-base PR is not
  claimable by `fleet_task_class._task_claimable`.
- A `Closes #N` hit whose base **is** master with N still open emits a scout
  warning (stale-queued), and does not suppress the task.
- Hermetic tests per `scripts/fleet/CLAUDE.md` §Authoring rules, including the
  master-base stale-queued arm as a distinct case from the non-master one.
- If route 2: `test_scope_shipped_reference.py` extended so the two writers'
  meanings can't drift, and both readers audited.

## Context / what was ruled out

- **Not** fixed by #2672's PR: verified by reading the predicate it ships —
  it matches against `repo_state["prs"]`, which `fetch_prs` populates with
  `state=open` only, so no merged record is ever in scope for it.
- `pr["closes_issues"]` (derived at fetch time, `fleet-state-scout:369`) is
  the right field for either route — it already survives the body-pop and the
  304 reuse of body-stripped records (#2442). Neither route needs a new parse.
- Filed **unlabeled** deliberately: the fix surface is fleet machinery and
  this is a structural read, not a fired incident, so it does not clear the
  agent-approved lane's higher bar (TASK-FILING.md §Agent-approved follow-up
  lane) — and "design-direction change" is a routed-elsewhere class besides.
  Needs `human:approved` before it can queue.

sample.title: Consumer pause-assign-resume may leave some partitions permanently paused
sample.body:
We hit this bug in production today, but seems to be an extremely rare one. Claude helped with the investigation, but it was checked by a human (myself); I'm not familiar with librdkafka internals though.

For context, we have a Rust application that handles rebalance events by first pausing all partitions in the assignment, and after assign/unassign, resuming them. We do this because we forward all partitions to separate queues, and without pause some fetch events may end up in the main queue during the window between assign and queue split.

The issue triggered during an application restart: it was assigned 426 partitions as expected, and began fetching from all of them except one. For that one partition, the consumer position remained invalid, and we never received any events from it. `rd_kafka_queue_length()` remained 0 for its queue the entire time. No logs, no errors.

The below is Claude's analysis, edited for brevity and readability:

Every pause/resume allocates a per-toppar version barrier and the op is discarded if it turns out to be stale:

- `rd_kafka_toppar_op_pause_resume()`: checks `IS_PAUSED`, then `version = rd_kafka_toppar_version_new_barrier(rktp)` (atomic increment), then enqueues the `OP_PAUSE` on `rktp_ops`.
- `rd_kafka_toppar_op_serve()`: `outdated = rko->rko_version < rktp->rktp_op_version`: if outdated, `rd_kafka_op_reply(rko, ERR__OUTDATED)` and return. The pause/resume is never applied. This applies to `OP_PAUSE`, `OP_FETCH_START` and `OP_SEEK` alike.
- `rd_kafka_toppar_op_fetch_start()` allocates its own barrier the same way, and it is enqueued by the cgrp/assignment thread, asynchronously, as the bulk `OffsetFetch` replies for the new assignment come back. That is happening for all 426 partitions at exactly the moment your main thread is walking the same 426 partitions calling pause, split, resume.

Version allocation and enqueue are not atomic together, so for one toppar you can get: `RESUME` allocates v12 → cgrp allocates v13 for `FETCH_START` and enqueues it => `RESUME(v12)` enqueued behind it => toppar thread serves `FETCH_START(v13)` (sets `op_version=13, state active, next_fetch_start = committed offset`) => then `RESUME(v12)` is dropped as outdated.
`RD_KAFKA_TOPPAR_F_APP_PAUSE` is never cleared, so `rd_kafka_toppar_fetch_decide` never fetches. The mirror-image ordering drops the `FETCH_START` instead, leaving the toppar in state none, and the resume's rescue path only fires for active/offset-wait with an `INVALID` next_fetch_start, so it doesn't help there either.

And it's silent by construction: `rd_kafka_toppars_pause_resume()` sets `rktpar->err = NO_ERROR` unconditionally, waits for the replies without inspecting them, and returns `NO_ERROR`, so `resume(&assignment).unwrap()` succeeds even though one partition stayed paused. librdkafka itself flags the area as fragile: the resume path carries the comment "If partitions isn't paused, avoid bumping its version, as it'll result in resuming fetches from a stale next_fetch_start".

The issue looks similar to https://github.com/confluentinc/librdkafka/issues/2190, but the fix doesn't address this particular case: for partitions whose committed offset isn't known yet, the `FETCH_START` is not issued by `assign()` at all: the assignment machinery puts them on a pending list, sends an `OffsetFetchRequest`, and only enqueues `rd_kafka_toppar_op_fetch_start()` from the reply handler `rd_kafka_assignment_handle_OffsetFetch`, long after the blocking `assign()` has returned. That is exactly our pause => 426 splits => resume window.

Other related context:
- https://github.com/confluentinc/librdkafka/issues/5460: they hit the same version filter silently dropping things in the KIP-932 share path and fixed it by stamping version = 0, which `rd_kafka_op_version_outdated()` treats as never-outdated. Direct precedent for the fix we want: pause/resume is state, not offset-dependent, so it should never be version-filtered.
- https://github.com/confluentinc/librdkafka/issues/5113: partitions reported as remaining paused after a rebalance. Plausibly the same symptom, unresolved.

sample.title: FUSE: WAL truncate leaves stale UnlinkedData on live handles, corrupting the next SQLite checkpoint
sample.body:
A confirmed FUSE read-path defect causes silent SQLite data loss after two explicit WAL TRUNCATE checkpoints, even with the new `interactive + --append-log` configuration. Twelve insert commits succeed, but the second checkpoint persists only the first five rows.

**Root-cause confirmation is complete. The next agent should start with a focused regression test and the fix below; another pre-fix dev-cluster investigation is not required.** This issue includes real FUSE read-source logs, byte-for-byte page comparisons, the original DB/WAL snapshots in an embedded evidence bundle, and commit-pinned code links. Post-fix verification is still required.

Related: #876 (same data-loss symptom, different confirmed mechanism), #880/#882/#883 (prior fixes), and #888 (separate pattern parser defect). The working pattern here is `**/repro.db-wal`, not the non-matching `**/*-wal` pattern from #888.

| CLI source / main at validation | `cff6d294b452b54a964de2217c137af303602be9` |

| Workload runtime | Linux arm64, gVisor directfs, runsc `release-20260810.0` |
| Workload cluster | `dev-drive9-eks-ap-southeast-1` |
| Server | `dev-drive9-eks-us-east-1`, namespace `drive9-tidbcloud`, `drive9-server-lb`; server source `tidbcloud/fs@be48de3` |
| Tenant capability | `storage_capabilities.append_log_v1=true` |
| SQLite writer | Python 3.13.5 / SQLite 3.46.1 |
| SQLite pragmas | WAL, synchronous=FULL (2), wal_autocheckpoint=0, journal_size_limit=-1, busy_timeout=5000, page_size=4096 |
| Application writers | One SQLite connection, serial per-row commits |
| Native CSI failure case | `i876-interactive-wal` |
| Diagnostic confirmation case | `i876-trace-v1`, 2026-09-06 UTC |

The native CSI run first reproduced the loss with the exact optimized settings. Native CSI does not expose `--debug`; for read-source confirmation only, the **same unmodified image/binary** provided a separate privileged debug FUSE mount on the same node, with hostPID enabled. A static hostPath PV/PVC exposed that mount to a gVisor writer. This distinction matters: the trace run confirms the FUSE root cause; it does not claim an additional native CSI provisioning test. No production code or server was changed.

Mount settings used in both runs, with `--debug` added only for tracing:

```text
--supervise-foreground
--mode=fuse
--direct-mount-strict
--gvisor-compat=true
--allow-other
--profile coding-agent
--durability interactive
--append-log=**/repro.db-wal
--remote-only=**/tmp/**
--remote-only=**/.tmp/**
--attr-ttl 30s
--entry-ttl 30s
--dir-ttl 30s
--readdir-prefetch
--readdir-prefetch-max-files 64
--readdir-prefetch-max-file-bytes 50000
--readdir-prefetch-max-bytes 4194304
--writeback-batch-window 20ms
```

Fresh cache/local/perf directories and a previously unused remote directory were used. The remote endpoint remained the specified us-east-1 dev server. Credentials were supplied separately and are not included here.

#### Exact operation sequence

1. In a fresh gVisor workload directory, create `repro.db` and table `items(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, val TEXT)`.
2. Insert `val-0` through `val-4`, committing each insert separately.
3. Execute `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` (checkpoint A), require busy=0; same-connection and independent HTTP DB checks both show five rows.
4. Keep the same SQLite connection and sandbox alive. Insert `val-5` through `val-11`, again committing each insert separately.
5. Execute a second `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` (checkpoint B), again busy=0. The same connection reports twelve rows; independent HTTP already reports five.
6. Close and immediately reopen: only five rows. Sandbox exit does not repair the remote main DB. A separate native CSI fresh-volume reader in the preceding run also saw five rows.

The diagnostic probe paused at A and B using local `/tmp` gates while the coordinator waited for upload/commit queues to settle and fetched remote files. It did not close the SQLite connection between checkpoints. A separate HTTP observer, with no target PVC, downloaded DB/WAL bytes; collection did not introduce additional target FUSE readers. The trace has approximately 37 seconds between A and the next commit, and another approximately 37 seconds before close. The pauses are observation windows, not application retries.

sample.title: [Security] [CRITICAL] Remote code injection in Log4j
sample.body:
> [!NOTE]
> This issue was generated by the SRX Security Agent.

**Severity:** CRITICAL
**Type:** Application

## Problem Description
A critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, also known as Log4Shell) affects applications that use the Log4j logging framework through the package org.ops4j.pax.logging:pax-logging-log4j2. When attacker-controlled data is logged, JNDI lookups can be triggered that may load and execute arbitrary code from remote servers. This vulnerability has a CVSS score of 10.0 and is widely exploited in the wild.

## Remediation Guidance
Upgrade all dependencies that include Log4j to a secure version and remove any reliance on insecure JNDI-based lookups. Focus on updating org.ops4j.pax.logging:pax-logging-log4j2 to a fixed version (such as 2.0.11 or higher) that pulls in Log4j 2.16.0 or later. Review logging configuration files to ensure they do not re-enable legacy or unsafe Log4j behavior and avoid patterns that log untrusted user input without appropriate sanitization.

## Affected Resources
- UserMappingService

## Remediation Steps
1. Update the org.ops4j.pax.logging:pax-logging-log4j2 dependency to a version that includes Log4j 2.16.0 or higher in the build configuration for each affected service.
2. Add or update dependency management constraints so that all transitive Log4j dependencies resolve to a secure version and cannot be downgraded by other libraries.
3. Review Log4j and framework-specific logging configuration files to remove or disable any JNDI-based lookup features or legacy configuration that depends on remote lookups.
4. Adjust logging patterns so that untrusted user input is not logged in a way that could trigger dangerous lookups or deserialization paths.
5. Regenerate build artifacts for each affected service using the updated dependency and configuration settings.

## Validation Steps
1. Confirm the build files for each service resolve org.ops4j.pax.logging:pax-logging-log4j2 to a version that includes Log4j 2.16.0 or higher.
2. Review the dependency tree for each service to verify that no older or vulnerable Log4j versions remain as transitive dependencies.
3. Check logging configuration files to ensure no JNDI-based lookup features or remote lookup patterns remain enabled.
4. Verify that logging still functions correctly with the updated dependencies and configuration, focusing on critical authentication and business flows.
5. Confirm that build and deployment pipelines use the updated artifacts that contain the secure Log4j version.

## Copilot Instructions
### Do
- Locate the build configuration files for each affected service (for example, Maven pom.xml or Gradle build files) and update the org.ops4j.pax.logging:pax-logging-log4j2 dependency to a version that includes Log4j 2.16.0 or higher.
- Add dependency management or constraints to enforce the secure Log4j version across all modules in each service.
- Review and update logging configuration files to remove or disable any JNDI-based lookup features and to use safe logging patterns.
- Keep all existing non-security-related behavior unchanged while applying the minimal set of changes needed to mitigate CVE-2021-44228.

### Do Not
- Do not introduce new logging frameworks unless explicitly required by project standards.
- Do not remove logging statements that are needed for observability unless they directly contribute to the vulnerability.
- Do not downgrade any security-related dependencies or relax existing security configuration.
- Do not modify unrelated application code or configuration outside of logging and dependency management.

---

sample.body:
### Pre-submission checklist

- [x] This does not change user-facing behavior (commands, output, file formats, config)
- [x] I have searched existing issues — this has not already been filed

### What is the maintenance task?

Migrate 352 pre-existing ad hoc numeric `timeout`/`timeoutMs` literals across 126 test files to named constants, per the newly-enforced `local/no-adhoc-timeout-literal` ESLint rule (grandfathered into that rule's allowlist for now so it can ship without breaking CI).

### Type of maintenance

Test quality (coverage, patterns, runner)

### Current state

A new lint rule, `local/no-adhoc-timeout-literal` (`eslint-rules/no-adhoc-timeout-literal.cjs`, documented in `TESTING-STANDARDS.md` — "No ad hoc timeout literals" — and `TEST-EXAMPLES.md`), bans a bare numeric `timeout`/`timeoutMs` option value in test files: two independently-guessed copies of the same magic number can silently drift apart, or worse, collide exactly and produce a zero-margin race. That's not hypothetical — `gsd-core/bin/check-latest-version.cjs`'s `timeout: 15_000` and `tests/gsd-check-update-worker-atomic-cache.test.cjs`'s independent `timeoutMs: 15000` collided exactly and caused a real Windows CI failure on 2026-09-06 (fixed in PR #4428).

Rolling the rule out at `error` immediately (with no allowlist) would break `npm run lint:ci` on 126 pre-existing files. It ships instead with a full grandfather allowlist (`eslint-rules/no-adhoc-timeout-literal.allowlist.json`) — same rollout mechanics `local/no-unbounded-spawn` used (see CONTRIBUTING.md: introduced with an allowlist, migrated over several waves, allowlist deleted once every site was clean). The allowlist only ever ratchets down: a listed file with zero violations makes the rule itself report `staleAllowlistEntry`, so a fix can't be forgotten to be un-grandfathered.

Full per-file audit (352 violations across 126 files, generated by running the rule against `tests/` with an empty allowlist):

sample.title: Migrate STAC link generation to the new item API and migrate existing catalog items
sample.body:
> Part of the ecosystem cutover tracked in **EOPF-Explorer/coordination#304** (under epic EOPF-Explorer/coordination#287).
> Upstream change: **EOPF-Explorer/titiler-eopf#114**, staged on `/rstaging`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Do not start writing URLs yet.** The URL contract is not frozen. A third route level
> (`/collections/{cid}/items/{iid}/assets/{aid}`) is being added and the item viewer is being ported
> to `assets=`; neither is on the branch yet. Wait for the Phase A gate in coordination#304, then pick
> the target route shape. This issue records *what* must change and *where* — not the final syntax.

### The change, in short

| | Old | New |
|---|---|---|
| Band selection | `variables=/measurements/reflectance:b04` | `assets=reflectance\|bands=b04` (or, once it lands, `/assets/reflectance/…?bands=b04`) |
| Expression operands | Zarr paths (`/measurements/reflectance:b08`) | **positional** `b1`, `b2`, … over the bands named in `bands=` |

Verified on `/rstaging`: old syntax → **422**, `assets=reflectance|bands=b04,b03,b02` → **200**,
`assets=reflectance|bands=b08,b04&expression=(b1-b2)/(b1+b2)` → **200**.

The expression rule is the easy one to get wrong: operands are positional, not band names.

## Why

This repo writes the visualisation links for every item in the live catalogue, in the old
`variables=` syntax. When titiler-eopf#114 deploys, every `xyz`, `tilejson` and `thumbnail` href in
the catalogue stops working, and the `rel=viewer` link points at a route that changed shape.

This is the critical path of the maintenance window: **step 3 of the cutover, and the thing that sets
the window length.** Between the tiler deploy and the end of the catalog migration, every
already-registered item is broken.

## Two deliverables — both required

### (a) Link generation

- `scripts/register_v1.py`
  - L316 — S2 true-colour query, reused at L382 for the `thumbnail` asset
  - L294-297 — S1 GRD VH (`var_path = f"/{orbit_group}:vh"`)
  - L287 — the `rel=viewer` href; needs the new viewer's query once #114 restores it
  - L204-220 `_render_to_query()` — serialises `expression=` from `properties.renders` with Zarr-path
    operands; these become positional `b1`/`b2`
  - L408-422 `warm_thumbnail_cache()` — would otherwise warm 4xx responses
- `scripts/register_v0.py` — L117, L125, L144, L182, L188 (same patterns)
- `scripts/register_per_acquisition.py` L63-104
- `scripts/register_v1_s1_rtc.py` L60 — `rgb["expression"] = f"{vv};{vh};({vv})/({vh})"`
- `tests/unit/test_cache_warming.py:27`

### (b) Migration of already-registered items

New registrations alone are not enough — everything already in the catalogue carries the old syntax
and must be rewritten. Add a migration under `operator-tools/_migrate_catalog/migrations/` that
rewrites `variables=` → the new syntax on `xyz` / `tilejson` / `thumbnail` hrefs, and repairs
`rel=viewer`.

- `add_xyz_link.py` L9-54 is the pattern to follow — note it string-replaces on
  `/WebMercatorQuad/tilejson.json?` and carries the old query verbatim, so it needs updating too
- `align_visualization_links.py` L10 (`_ORDER = {"store": 0, "viewer": 1, …}`) already normalises
  link order and is the natural place to hook in

Representative fixtures showing what is in the catalogue today:
`stac/S2A_MSIL2A_20250831T103701_N0511_R008_T31TFL_20250831T145420.json` L49, L55, L112;
`stac/S2A_MSIL2A_20251008T100041_N0511_R122_T32TQM_20251008T122613.szeopf.json` L161, L179.

## Route choice

S2 true-colour and S1 VH each draw from a **single** asset, so the per-asset route
(`/collections/{cid}/items/{iid}/assets/{aid}`) is the likely target once the gate clears. Confirm in
coordination#304 before writing hrefs.

## Related

**#246 becomes actionable.** titiler-eopf#114 closes titiler-eopf#108, so the S1 RTC `tests-output`
store-path workaround can be reverted per that issue's revert contract. Worth doing in the same pass.

Stale references to the removed env vars, worth cleaning while here:
`claude-docs/plans/s1_grd_phase6_productionization.md` L249 and
`claude-docs/plans/subissue_4_end_to_end.md` L376 mention `TITILER_EOPF_STORE_URL`;
`subissue_4_end_to_end.md` L252 references `…/items/s1-rtc-31TCH/viewer`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No `variables=` in any generated link
- [ ] A freshly registered item renders `/info`, `tilejson` and `/preview` as HTTP 200 on `/rstaging`
      with no manual store copy
- [ ] The migration is dry-run against staging and its **runtime measured** — that number is the
      window length in coordination#304
- [ ] A migrated pre-existing item renders 200 on `/rstaging`
- [ ] `rel=viewer` resolves and renders
- [ ] PR is approved and held unmerged until the maintenance window
