sample.title: perf(runtime): Function.prototype.bind eagerly materializes name/length metadata, costing ~355x Node at every size
sample.body:
## What happened

On pinned Perry 9495bfc95e2a, a loop of `bound(a, b)` calls costs 2642.184 ms at 1M iterations versus Node's 7.487 ms — 352.87x — and the ratio is essentially flat from n=100 (364.36x) upward, so this is a fixed per-operation cost rather than a scaling problem. Checksums match at every size. `bind` is the most expensive of the three Function.prototype dispatch entry points by a factor of six; `call`/`apply` are filed separately because their cost sits in a different helper.

Measured against Node `v26.5.1` using Perry `perry 0.5.1531` at [`9495bfc95e2afcfb5a7cb535e440e61ec0722cb1`](https://github.com/PerryTS/perry/commit/9495bfc95e2afcfb5a7cb535e440e61ec0722cb1). This is evidence from that pinned revision, not a claim that current main was remeasured. First reproduce on current main; if it is already fixed, identify the fixing commit and attach the comparison.

## Measurements

Times are median milliseconds per workload invocation. Ratios are Perry/Node. A correctness or timeout classification takes precedence over performance; successful smaller-size timings on those rows are diagnostic evidence.

### `function-bind` — SEVERE

| n | Node ms / status | Perry ms / status | ratio | Node checksum | Perry checksum |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 100 | 0.000445 | 0.161965 | 363.63× | 53206851 | 53206851 |
| 1000 | 0.004237 | 1.509089 | 356.13× | 509020824 | 509020824 |
| 10000 | 0.042677 | 16.548625 | 387.76× | 6312813 | 6312813 |
| 100000 | 0.436631 | 366.727542 | 839.90× | 65781663 | 65781663 |
| 1000000 | 7.487333 | 2642.183958 | 352.89× | 468838303 | 468838303 |

Log(time)/log(n) least-squares slopes: Perry **1.081**, Node **1.046**, delta **0.035**.

Workload: n calls with two numeric arguments and a nontrivial this receiver; apply/bind include their natural per-call argument/wrapper allocation.

## What is expected / acceptance criteria

- [ ] Rerun the complete reproducer on the candidate release build and Node at 100, 1k, 10k, 100k and 1M iterations. Checksums must match at every size, and the Perry/Node ratio must improve materially at every size rather than only at the largest.
- [ ] Remove the per-bind eager construction of the `"bound …"` name string and of the two constant-key property-attribute records. Demonstrate with bounded allocation counts or profiling that a bind which never reads `.name`/`.length` performs no runtime-string allocation for the name and no `String` allocation for the literal keys.
- [ ] Preserve the full spec surface with regression coverage: `f.bind().name === 'bound f'`, chained `f.bind().bind().name === 'bound bound f'`, an `Object.defineProperty(f, 'name', …)` override observed through the bound function, `name`/`length` non-enumerable in `for-in` and absent from `Object.keys`, `length` equal to `max(0, target.length - boundArgs.length)`, and the +Infinity / beyond-u32 length path at lines 560-570.
- [ ] Keep the existing Test262 bind coverage green, including `bind/instance-name*` and the class-ref (`target_class_id`) branch where the target is a constructor rather than a heap closure.
- [ ] Verify moving-GC safety: the target value, bound `this`, and partial-argument array must stay rooted across every allocating call, and any lazily-derived name must not retain a stale closure address across a copying collection.

## Implementation to inspect

**Hypothesis:** Hypothesis from the measured source: `js_function_bind` builds the full spec-visible function metadata on every single bind, even though the overwhelmingly common case never reads `.name` or `.length` off the bound function.

In [bound.rs:463](https://github.com/PerryTS/perry/blob/9495bfc95e2afcfb5a7cb535e440e61ec0722cb1/crates/perry-runtime/src/closure/dispatch/bound.rs#L463) each call performs, in order: a partial-argument array allocation through `js_array_alloc` plus one `js_array_push_f64` per bound argument (lines 513-522); a 3-capture closure allocation (line 525); a `.length` resolution that goes through `closure_get_own_dynamic_prop(target, "length")` (line 535); then the part that dominates. Line 588 runs `format!("bound {target_name}")`, allocating a Rust `String` and copying the target name, followed by `js_string_from_bytes` (line 590) to allocate a second runtime string. Line 592 inserts that through `closure_set_dynamic_prop(bound, "name", …)`. Lines 597-606 then call `set_builtin_property_attrs` twice, each of which allocates another Rust `String` for the literal key (`"name".to_string()`, `"length".to_string()`) and inserts into a side table keyed by the closure address.

So a single `bind` performs at minimum two runtime-string allocations, two transient Rust `String` allocations for constant keys, one array allocation, one closure allocation, and three address-keyed side-table inserts. Node stores a bound function's `name` and `length` lazily and materializes them only when read. This is source attribution consistent with the flat ~355x ratio; it is not a profiler result, and the relative weight of the individual allocations above has not been measured.

The target-name read at line 579 (`read_function_name_property`, falling back to `function_name_for_ptr`) is itself only needed to build the eagerly-stored `"bound …"` string. If the name is derived on demand, the target closure pointer already captured in slot 0 is enough to reconstruct it.

Note for whoever picks this up: the two `set_builtin_property_attrs` calls exist to keep `name`/`length` non-enumerable (Test262 `bind/instance-name*`), so they cannot simply be deleted — the attributes have to survive whatever lazy scheme replaces them. `js_closure_alloc` already carries a builtin-length channel (`set_builtin_closure_length`, line 561) that does not allocate a key string.

- [crates/perry-runtime/src/closure/dispatch/bound.rs](https://github.com/PerryTS/perry/blob/9495bfc95e2afcfb5a7cb535e440e61ec0722cb1/crates/perry-runtime/src/closure/dispatch/bound.rs): `js_function_bind`

Source reading narrows

sample.title: apply_patch: 7-file patch rejected because one scene.js hunk's context (the three.js import line) did not match; error gives no hint what differs
sample.body:
## What happened

A builder step called `apply_patch` on seven files at once and the whole call was rejected:

```
apply_patch src/garden.js, src/shell.js, src/dimensions.js, src/materials.js, src/facades.js, src/balconies.js, src/scene.js
workspace error: patch rejected, nothing was written: src/scene.js, hunk 1: context not found (starting at 'import * as THREE from 'three';'); the ' ' and '-' lines must match the current file, read it again
```

Six files applied cleanly in the dry run; one hunk in `src/scene.js` failed on its very first context line, the three.js import. That line is in every scene entry point, so the hunk text itself is almost certainly what differs from the file (quote style, a `//` comment on the same line, extra imports on the line, or the model wrote the hunk from memory / a stale read after it had rewritten `scene.js` earlier in the step).

## Where

- `backend/src/housegen/agent/patch.py`: `_find` matches hunks exact, then ignoring trailing whitespace, then ignoring all whitespace. Nothing else is tolerated, and the error message does not show what the file actually has at the nearest candidate line.
- `backend/src/housegen/agent/patch.py::apply_patch`: everything is computed first and the whole patch is dropped on the first failing hunk (documented as intended, atomic).

## Why it matters

The all-or-nothing rejection turns one wrong context line into a lost step and a full re-emission of seven files (xhigh effort, lots of output tokens). With the step budget and cost per builder pass, this is expensive, and the model often retries with the same hunk because the message does not tell it *what* differs.

## To do

1. Reproduce from the job log: recover the patch text and the `scene.js` content at that moment (both are in the builder trace) and see which normalisation would have matched. Possible cases: `'three'` vs `"three"`, a trailing comment, a differently spelled import (`import { ... } from 'three'`), CRLF, or a stale view of the file.
2. Make the error actionable: quote the closest line(s) in the file (e.g. the first line that shares the same leading token, with a small diff), instead of only the hunk's first line.
3. Consider a per-file result: apply the files whose hunks match, report the failing file(s) with the rejected hunk, so the model only has to resend one file. Keep it atomic *per file*. If atomic across files is kept on purpose, say so in the tool description so the model sends independent files in separate calls.
4. Decide whether `_find` should also try a quote-normalised / comment-stripped match for context lines, or whether that hides real mismatches.
5. Add a regression test in `backend/tests` for whichever mismatch case (1) turns up.

sample.title: feat: P2-WP012 Production Orchestrator & Staged Approval State Machine
sample.body:
## Work Package Contract — P2-WP012

**Title:** Production Orchestrator & Staged Approval State Machine
**Owner authorization:** APPROVED in chat on 2026-09-06
**Canonical branch:** `main`
**Live starting main HEAD:** `3be8ffed28f8807ae89bab22fb64a8018a8fbdb7`

> Goal: make Orbis workflow orchestration backend-owned, mode-aware, approval-gated, resumable and genuinely usable from the browser. Do not build a cosmetic wizard or frontend-only state machine.

## Product truth to preserve
- Orbis = cloud-first, provider-independent AI Video Production Orchestrator / Production Control Plane.
- Core V1 modes: STORY / SHORT / LOOP / SCENE.
- Story is NOT mandatory for every mode.
- Automation-first + guided flexibility + explicit human authority.
- Full history / auditable changes / no silent history loss.
- Expensive generation remains approval/cost gated.
- Reuse durable queue, retry/resume, locks, usage ledger and BatchRun from closed WPs.
- Vidu remains current registered VideoProvider; no direct provider calls from orchestrator.

## Current problem to solve
Current UI performs several stage transitions itself and generic project PATCH can directly mutate `Project.status`. That makes workflow truth client-driven and allows invalid/out-of-order transitions. WP012 must establish a canonical backend orchestration boundary and make frontend consume it.

## In scope

### 1. Canonical production-stage model
Define one backend-owned stage/state vocabulary and transition graph for the currently implemented V1 production path, mode-aware for STORY / SHORT / LOOP / SCENE.

The model must distinguish at minimum:
- planning/generated state vs approved state
- active generation state
- blocked/recovery state where applicable
- final review/completion states already present

Do not force SHORT/LOOP/SCENE through Story.

### 2. ProductionOrchestrator service
Implement a canonical service that owns:
- current production state evaluation
- allowed transitions
- transition preconditions
- approval transitions
- pause / continue / resume semantics
- next-best-action computation
- orchestration command dispatch to existing services
- truthful blocked reason(s)

No duplicated transition tables/rules across frontend/endpoints/services.

### 3. Backend-owned transition APIs
Add canonical APIs for:
- read orchestration state / current stage / available actions / next recommended action
- execute an orchestration action
- approve/reject/revise stage where applicable
- read transition/audit history

Generic `PATCH /projects/{id}` must no longer be a bypass for controlled production-stage transitions. Non-stage project metadata updates must continue to work.

### 4. Mode-aware flow
Support actual current V1 structures:
- STORY: Story -> Story approval -> Storyboard -> Storyboard approval -> Shot Plan -> Shot Plan approval -> production generation
- SHORT: compact structure/scene path; no mandatory Story
- LOOP: loop spec/shot path; no mandatory Story/Script
- SCENE: scene/shot path; no mandatory Story

Use existing generation/planning services where possible. Do not implement WP013 ImageProvider.

### 5. Automation modes
Add provider-neutral orchestration preference with clear semantics:
- MANUAL: user explicitly triggers every stage/action
- ASSISTED: system recommends next action and may automate non-chargeable safe planning actions only with truthful UI
- AUTO: may continue through eligible non-blocked stages according to policy, but MUST stop at mandatory human approval/cost gates and must never silently trigger chargeable generation where approval is required

Persist automation preference at project level in a backward-compatible way.

### 6. Approval / pause / resume safety
- Approval state must be backend-authoritative.
- Invalid/out-of-order transition -> fail closed with clear reason.
- Repeated approve/continue requests must be idempotent/repeat-safe.
- Resume after interruption must evaluate repository/database truth, not blindly replay prior steps.
- Locked entities, reconciliation-required work, active jobs, budget caps and existing completed work must remain respected.
- Do not overwrite historical approved/generated assets.

### 7. Audit history
Persist lightweight auditable transition history containing at minimum:
- project_id
- from_state
- to_state or attempted action
- action
- actor/source
- result (APPLIED / NO_OP / BLOCKED / FAILED)
- reason/code
- created_at

Avoid destructive history updates.

### 8. Browser UX that is genuinely usable
Replace frontend-owned stage mutation logic with canonical orchestrator API use.

UI must show:
- current stage in plain language
- one clear primary Recommended Next Action
- secondary actions where valid
- why an action is blocked
- review/approve controls when required
- automation mode (Manual / Assisted / Auto) with understandable descriptions
- truthful progress when jobs are queued/running
- safe recovery action for failure/reconciliation states

Do not expose provider/model complexity in the normal path.

### 9. Existing queue integration
Video generation actions must route through existing canonical generation / BatchResume / durable queue services rather than creating another queue or client-side loops.

The orchestrator may initiate existing bounded operations, but WP011 safety/idempotency/cost behavior must not be weakened.

### 10. Practical end-to-end tests
Implement focused backend + frontend/integration tests proving the system is usable, including at minimum:
- STORY happy path to approved shot plan and video dispatch gate
- SHORT flow without Story
- LOOP flow without Story/Script
- SCENE flow without Story
- invalid stage skip rejected
- generic project PATCH cannot bypass controlled stage transition
- repeated approval/action is idempotent / no duplicate work
- AUTO stops at mandatory approval/cost gate
- ASSISTED recommends but does not silently perform chargeable work
- resume after partial state chooses correct next action
- active/recon

🤖 This issue was generated by Claude on behalf of @keddie.

`docs/architecture.md` mentions `kuilt-nw` twice (the `NWPathMonitor` capability discussion around L331, and the 16 MiB frame-limit story at L374), so it isn't wholly stale. But the **Near/Far topology overview** at the top still presents Apple's fabric as Multipeer Connectivity:

- **L17** — "the WebSocket fabric and a future N-peer Multipeer mesh can share one contract." The N-peer Apple mesh is not future and is not Multipeer; it shipped as `kuilt-nw`.
- **L25** — Near is "(Multipeer, WebRTC data channel, Android Nearby)".

sample.title: add_episodes and delete_episodes release the episodic-memory reference before the write runs: the coroutine is awaited after async with exits
sample.body:
### What happened

`MemMachine.add_episodes` opens the session's episodic memory in an `async with` block, but only *creates* the write coroutine inside it. The coroutine is awaited after the block has exited (`packages/server/src/memmachine_server/main/memmachine.py`, as of `98f3cde` speedkick):

```python
async with episodic_memory_manager.open_or_create_episodic_memory(...) as episodic_session:   # line 767
    tasks.append(episodic_session.add_memory_episodes(episodes))                             # line 775
...
await asyncio.gather(*tasks)                                                                 # line 788
```

`delete_episodes` has the same shape: `open_episodic_memory` at line 1211, `episodic_session.delete_episodes(...)` appended at 1214, gathered at 1219.

A coroutine object does no work until it is awaited, so the whole episodic write runs after the context manager's `finally` has run. That `finally` calls `_update_cache` → `InstanceLRUCache.release_ref` (`episodic_memory/episodic_memory_manager.py:286-289`, `:108-113`; `episodic_memory/instance_lru_cache.py:193`), so the reference count has already dropped when the write starts.

### Why it matters

The reference count is what protects an instance in use:

- `delete_episodic_session` refuses with `SessionInUseError` only while `ref_count > 0` (`episodic_memory_manager.py:304-307`), and `close_session` does the same (lines 360-364). With the count already released, a concurrent project delete or close can proceed and close the instance while `add_memory_episodes` or `delete_episodes` is still writing through it.
- `InstanceLRUCache.clean_old_instance` (`instance_lru_cache.py:206`) closes nodes whose `ref_count` is 0 once they pass `max_lifetime`. It skips an instance mid-write only if the reference is still held.

This was found by reading the code, not by reproducing a failure; the window is the duration of the episodic write.

### Expected

Await the episodic work while the reference is held. For `add_episodes`, either move the `async with` so it encloses the `gather`, or create the task inside the block and await everything before leaving it:

```python
async with episodic_memory_manager.open_or_create_episodic_memory(...) as episodic_session:
    tasks.append(episodic_session.add_memory_episodes(episodes))
    ...  # semantic task
    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
```

The same change applies to `delete_episodes`.

*Investigated and written by Claude (Claude Code), filed from the account of the user who commissioned the investigation.*

sample.title: Backend scheduler crashes with broadcast_shapes ValueError in BatchRotatingKVCache.merge under concurrent requests with shared prefix
sample.body:
**Environment**

LM Studio backend: app-mlx-generate-mac14-arm64@34 (mlx_engine, Python 3.11)
Model: qwen/qwen3-4b-2507 (MLX, 4-bit)
Hardware: Mac mini, Apple Silicon, 16 GB
Server settings at crash: Max Concurrent Predictions 16, context 32768, KV cache quantization off. Also reproduces at the default 4 slots / 8192 ctx.

**Reproduction**

8 concurrent OpenAI-format streaming clients, each in a tight loop: identical ~2000-token prompt prefix + short unique suffix, max_tokens: 64, temperature: 0, no delay between turns. Crashes within ~60 seconds. Reproduced in two independent runs (23 and 10 failed requests respectively; 4 model crashes total). At concurrency ≤4 the same workload runs clean (hundreds of requests, zero errors).

**Observed**

Client side: streams open (HTTP 200) then deliver zero content chunks; some requests receive HTTP 500; surviving requests see TTFT p95 ~18s (reload gap). The model then auto-reloads — with default settings, discarding the user-configured slot count and context length (see "Impact").

Server log (repeated 23×, followed by 4× "The model has crashed without additional information. (Exit code: null)"):

[batched_model_kit][ERROR]: Encountered fatal exception in the backend scheduler:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ... mlx_engine/model_kit/batched_model_kit.py ... self._generate()
  ... mlx_lm/generate.py ... prompt_responses, generation_responses = batch_generator.next()
  ... mlx_lm/generate.py ... self._prompt_batch.extend(self._make_batch(n))
  ... mlx_lm/generate.py ... return PromptProcessingBatch(
  ... mlx_lm/generate.py ... self.prompt_cache = _merge_caches(caches)
  ... mlx_lm/generate.py ... batch_cache.append(caches[0][i].merge([c[i] for c in caches]))
  ... mlx_lm/models/cache.py ... return BatchRotatingKVCache.merge(caches)
  ... mlx_lm/models/cache.py ...
      keys[i : i + 1, :, p : p + l] = c._temporal_order(c.keys)[..., -l:, :]
ValueError: [broadcast_shapes] Shapes (1,8,348,128) and (1,8,907,128) cannot be broadcast.

**Analysis (best effort)**

The scheduler batches prompt-processing for concurrent requests and merges their per-request prompt caches. When the cached prefixes have different retained lengths (here 348 vs 907 tokens — plausibly different truncation / rotation states of the same shared prefix), BatchRotatingKVCache.merge writes one cache's keys into a slot sized for another and the shape mismatch raises, killing the whole scheduler rather than the one request.

**Impact**

All in-flight requests fail (empty streams / 500s).
The model auto-reloads with default load settings, silently discarding the configured Max Concurrent Predictions and context length — so a server that was configured for 16 slots continues running at 4 after recovery. For unattended server deployments this is a second bug: crash recovery causes silent configuration drift.

**Suggested severity**: high for headless/server use — the trigger (several concurrent clients sharing a prompt prefix) is the normal shape of agentic traffic behind a gateway.

sample.title: [BUG] Overview "Recent alerts" card builds monitor links with the literal string `dataSourceId=undefined`
sample.body:
## What is the bug?

With `data_source.enabled: true`, clicking an alert in the **Recent alerts** card on the Dashboards Overview page does not open the monitor. The page fails with:

```
Saved object [data-source/undefined] not found
```

The generated link carries the **literal string** `undefined` as the data source id:

```
#/monitors/<monitor_id>?&type=query&dataSourceId=undefined
```

That string then survives into the app's state and is forwarded to the backend. Over a 6-hour window a single deployment logged 34 requests of these two shapes:

```
GET /api/alerting/monitors/<id>?dataSourceId=undefined
GET /api/alerting/monitors?dataSourceId=undefined&from=0&...
```

## How can one reproduce the bug?

1. Deploy OpenSearch Dashboards with `data_source.enabled: true` and at least one data source registered.
2. Have at least one alert so the Overview page's **Recent alerts** card is not empty.
3. Open the Overview page and click any alert's trigger name in that card.
4. Observe the error. Inspect the link target: it ends in `&dataSourceId=undefined`.

The card does not need a data source to be manually picked: the failure happens with the card's own default (auto-resolved) selection.

## What is the root cause?

Two layers, both required.

**1. A stale closure in the card.** `createAlertDetailsHeader` reads `dataSource?.id`, but its `useCallback` dependency array only lists `agentAvailable`:

`public/components/DataSourceAlertsCard/DataSourceAlertsCard.tsx#L68-L101`

```jsx
const createAlertDetailsHeader = useCallback((alert) => {
  ...
  const url = getURL(monitorUrl, dataSource?.id);   // L74
  ...
      datasourceId={dataSource?.id}                 // L83
  ...
}, [agentAvailable]);                               // L101
```

`dataSource` is local state declared as `useState<DataSourceOption>()` (`DataSourceAlertsCard.tsx#L30`), so it is `undefined` on mount, and the card's own `DataSourceSelectable` only resolves the default selection asynchronously. Because `dataSource` is not a dependency, the callback is never recreated when the selection arrives.

The invariant is: **the callback freezes whatever `dataSource` held at the last `agentAvailable` change, or at mount if it never changes.** So the link is permanently broken whenever the data source resolves after that point. Two orderings produce that:

* `getIsAgentConfigured` resolves to the initial value `false` (no assistant agent configured). React bails out of the re-render, the callback is never regenerated, and it stays frozen on the mount-time `undefined`.
* `agentAvailable` genuinely flips `false → true`, but the agent-config round trip settles **before** `DataSourceSelectable` has resolved its default. The callback is regenerated while `dataSource` is still `undefined` and then never again. This ordering is the common one: the agent-config check is a single request, while the selector has to list saved objects and read the default-data-source setting first.

Re-renders keep happening in both cases (the alerts fetch effect at `L34-L51` runs again with the new `dataSource` and calls `setAlerts`), and each re-render calls the *stale* callback, so every rendered link is broken.

Note the contrast one screen up in the same file: the alerts fetch already falls back correctly with `dataSource?.id || ''` (`L40`), and the sibling effect correctly depends on `[dataSource?.id]` (`L60`). So the card fetches alerts from the right cluster while linking to `undefined`.

**2. `getURL` interpolates without a guard.**

`public/pages/utils/helpers.js#L58-L60`

```js
export function getURL(url, dataSourceId) {
  return dataSourceEnabled() ? `${url}&dataSourceId=${dataSourceId}` : url;
}
```

`undefined` is stringified into the query string.

**3. The string then propagates.** On the target page, `parseQueryStringAndGetDataSource` reads it back as a real id, `updateBreadcrumbs` accepts it because it is `!== undefined` (`public/pages/Main/Main.js#L91-L105`), and `resolveAndSetDataSource` (`Main.js#L68-L88`) stores it in the data source service before attempting to resolve it, so the bad value is retained even though the client-side resolution fails. It is then passed down as `landingDataSourceId` to the monitor detail links.

Server side, the guard is falsy-based:

`server/services/MDSEnabledClientService.ts#L113-L116`

```ts
const dataSourceId = (request.query as any).dataSourceId;
if (!this.dataSourceEnabled || !dataSourceId) {
  return this.osDriver.asScoped(request).callAsCurrentUser;
}
```

An absent or empty `dataSourceId` is falsy and falls back to the local cluster, but the *non-empty string* `"undefined"` is truthy, so the request proceeds to `#L127`:

```ts
return context.dataSource.opensearch.legacy.getClient(dataSourceId.toString()).callAPI;
```

That hands the string to OpenSearch Dashboards core's `data_source` client pool, which looks it up as a saved object id, and that lookup is what raises the reported `Saved object [data-source/undefined] not found`.

## Why this is not a deleted / missing data source

* Every `data-source` saved object in the affected deployment exists, and there are no dangling references to any of them.
* The failing id is not a real id at all: it is the 9-character string `undefined`, i.e. the result of template-interpolating a JS `undefined`.
* An actually-absent selection would serialize as an absent or empty parameter, which the falsy guard above already treats as "local cluster" and which never reaches a saved object lookup.

## Proposed fix

1. Add the missing dependency so the callback is regenerated when the selection resolves:
   `}, [agentAvailable, dataSource?.id]);` in `DataSourceAlertsCard.tsx#L101`.
2. Make `getURL` refuse to serialize an unresolved selection, falling back to the empty string:
   ```js
   return `${url}&dataSourceId=${dataSourceId ?? ''}`;
   ```
   The empty string is this repo's declared representation of the local cluster: `LocalCluster` is defined as `{ label: 'Local clust

sample.title: [P0 security] installer payload commits must be descriptor-relative and resist parent-directory swap escapes
sample.body:
> **Migrated from ImL1s/resume-skills#31**
> Originally created: 2026-07-25T20:08:58Z

## Summary

Payload destination containment currently relies on:

```python
dest = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(root, safe_rel))
commonpath(dest, real_root) == real_root
```

followed later by path-based operations such as:

- `os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(dest), exist_ok=True)`
- `os.replace(stage_file, dest)`
- `os.remove(dest)`
- no-follow open of the final source path only

This validates the resolved path at one moment but does not pin intermediate parent directories. A parent beneath the skill root can be replaced with a symlink after containment/classification and before commit, redirecting a payload replacement, backup, rollback, uninstall, or restore outside the selected root.

This is a **P0 local path-escape/write/delete vulnerability class** in the payload transaction plane.

Audit baseline: `main` / v0.3.3 (`52e881b`). #21 covers the `.portable-resume` control plane; this issue covers installed payload paths beneath the skill root.

## Affected code

- `transaction.py::_dest_under_root`
- `plan_install` destination classification
- `_classify_dest`
- `execute_install` staging/backup/commit/orphan removal
- `_copy_regular_nofollow`
- checkpoint capture and restore
- rollback/recovery
- `verify_root`
- `uninstall_claim`
- empty-directory cleanup where path identity matters

## Example race

Given target:

```text
<root>/resume-codex/SKILL.md
```

1. plan/classification resolves `<root>/resume-codex` as an ordinary directory inside root
2. an injected hook or concurrent process renames that directory away
3. it creates `<root>/resume-codex -> <outside>`
4. installer calls `os.replace(stage, <root>/resume-codex/SKILL.md)`
5. pathname resolution follows the new parent symlink and writes `<outside>/SKILL.md`

Checking only whether the final destination itself is a symlink does not prevent symlinked parent traversal.

The same class can affect backup/rollback copies and uninstall deletion.

## Required security model

- root identity is pinned for the transaction
- every payload path component is traversed descriptor-relative without following symlinks/reparse redirects
- parent directories created by the installer are created and reopened through pinned descriptors
- classification and commit refer to the same expected target identity/state
- a changed/missing/replaced parent or target causes conflict/busy/recovery-required, not an outside operation
- no install, verify, uninstall, rollback, or recovery operation can escape the selected root through path replacement
- user-owned symlinked Skill paths are rejected rather than followed, even when they currently resolve inside root

## Recommended implementation

### Step 1: Reuse a pinned root filesystem abstraction

Extend the #21 control-store design into an installer root abstraction with operations such as:

```text
open_parent_beneath(rel, create=False)
lstat_beneath(rel)
open_regular_beneath(rel, nofollow=True)
replace_from_stage_beneath(rel, expected_identity=...)
unlink_regular_beneath(rel, expected_digest=...)
mkdirs_beneath(rel_parent)
```

Traverse each component using directory file descriptors/handles and no-follow flags. Reject `..`, absolute paths, symlinks, and non-directory components.

Do not resolve a path once and then perform later ambient pathname operations.

### Step 2: Bind plan classifications to identities

For every existing destination classified during the locked replan, record bounded expected state:

- absent, or
- device/inode/type/size/mtime/content digest (POSIX), with platform equivalent
- expected ownership/manifest entry

Immediately before replace/delete, verify the target through the pinned parent descriptor still matches the classified identity. Unknown drift returns `E_INSTALL_CONFLICT` or `E_RECOVERY_REQUIRED` according to transaction phase.

### Step 3: Safe atomic commit

Stage files remain installer-owned regular files. Commit should:

- open/pin destination parent beneath root
- ensure final basename is not a directory/symlink/special file
- verify expected state
- atomically rename/replace into that pinned parent using descriptor-relative/platform-safe primitives where available
- fsync file/parent according to #21 policy

If Python APIs lack a direct portable primitive, implement narrow OS-specific helpers and fail closed on unsupported platforms rather than falling back to unsafe path resolution.

### Step 4: Apply to every lifecycle operation

The same beneath-root primitive must cover:

- backup of foreign conflicts
- rollback snapshots and restore
- orphan removal during upgrade
- checkpoint capture/compensation
- verify hashing
- uninstall deletion
- recovery restore/removal

Fixing only the forward install commit leaves delete/restore escape paths.

### Step 5: Directory cleanup

Empty-directory cleanup may enumerate only known ancestors of owned paths, but each removal must revalidate the directory beneath the pinned root and reject symlink/replacement drift.

## Regression tests

Use deterministic hooks between classification, snapshot, and operation.

### Commit escapes

- [ ] swap `resume-x` parent to symlink outside before `os.replace`; outside sentinel remains unchanged
- [ ] swap nested `.portable-resume/runtime/...` parent similarly
- [ ] replace final regular target with symlink before commit; reject
- [ ] replace parent with another in-root directory; detect identity drift

### Backup/rollback/recovery

- [ ] parent swap before foreign backup cannot read outside file
- [ ] parent swap before rollback restore cannot write outside
- [ ] malicious journal/rollback rel path cannot escape
- [ ] compensation refuses unexpected parent identity and reports recovery required

### Verify/uninstall

- [ ] verify cannot hash a file reached through a swapped parent symlink
- [ ] uninstall cannot delete outside through a parent symlink
- [ ] empty-dir cleanup cannot remove redirected directories

sample.title: Proto internal-browser playback race cross-wires source state and breaks all three fixed-folder videos
sample.body:
## Summary

Reproduced on July 28, 2026 in the Codex in-app browser at `https://proto.alphacompose.com/` while signed in as `me@jamiep.org`.

The current proto failure is no longer the earlier universal `POST /v1/drive/playback-analyses` `502` from #172. Playback analysis now completes for at least some selections, but the proto page races async responses across source switches and corrupts the active file state. In practice that leaves all three fixed-folder videos unplayable in the internal browser.

## Reproduction

1. Open `https://proto.alphacompose.com/` in the in-app browser.
2. Select each of the three fixed-folder sources from the left-hand list.
3. Watch the `Playback preparation` and `Range and buffering` debug panels while switching files.

## What happens

- `DJI_20260726091205_0070_D.MP4` ends in page status `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'playbackUrl')` with `state.session = null`.
- `GX011925.MP4` and `IMG_0435.MOV` show cross-wired debug state: the selected file is current, but `analysis`, `timing`, `session.contentType`, `session.size`, and `playbackUrl` can belong to a previous source.
- The page then probes or loads a stale playback URL and the range probe reports `500`, `contentType: text/html`, `contentLength: "0"`.
- All three appear broken to the user even though the underlying failure is the client state machine, not one common per-file media fact.

## Diagnosis

`src/agg/proto/core.clj` has a race in `selectSource(...)`.

- The proto page resets shared mutable `state`, then fires async requests for playback analysis, recording-clock inspection, playback session creation, and range probing.
- Unlike the main UI flow in `src/agg/ui/core.clj`, the proto flow has no generation / stale-response guard.
- If the user switches files before the previous async chain settles, late responses overwrite `state.analysis`, `state.timing`, `state.session`, and `state.rangeProbe` for the newly selected file.
- That directly explains the observed null dereference and the mismatched session payloads.

Relevant code:

- `src/agg/proto/core.clj:232` - async `selectSource(source)` mutates shared state with no generation guard.
- `src/agg/ui/core.clj:1187` - main UI `loadDrivePlayback(file)` already uses `const generation = ++playbackGeneration` and abandons stale completions.

## Evidence

Observed in the in-app browser after exercising the live page:

- `DJI_20260726091205_0070_D.MP4`: top status becomes `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'playbackUrl')`.
- `GX011925.MP4`: selected file is `GX011925.MP4`, but debug state carried a session with `contentType: "video/quicktime"` and `size: 5666308933` from another source.
- `IMG_0435.MOV`: selected file is `IMG_0435.MOV`, but debug state carried a session with `contentType: "video/mp4"` and `size: 828331628` from another source.
- Range probe for the corrupted session path returns `500` with HTML, not media bytes.

Cloud Run check:

- `agg-proto` is serving revision `agg-proto-00004-pkq`.
- No corresponding `severity>=ERROR` service logs were present during this repro window, which further points to the client-side race as the primary fault.

## Expected

Changing source should invalidate prior async completions. Only the latest selected source should be allowed to write `analysis`, `timing`, `session`, `rangeProbe`, and `player.src`.

## Likely fix

Mirror the guard already used in `src/agg/ui/core.clj`:

- add a monotonically increasing selection generation,
- capture it at the start of `selectSource`,
- bail out after each awaited step when the generation is stale,
- avoid dereferencing `state.session.playbackUrl` unless the active generation still owns that session,
- ideally reset or ignore late media events from superseded selections.

## Relation

- Follow-up to #172, which described the earlier analysis-stage `502` behavior.
- Related to #169 because the proto page still misreports the real failure mode to the user.

sample.title: Implement OPFS and SQLite-WASM (drift) persistence in a Worker
sample.body:
<!-- sn-key: SN-WEB-008 -->
**Key:** `SN-WEB-008` · **Priority:** P1 · **Type:** feature · **Size:** L · **SDLC:** implementation
**Platforms:** web · **Areas:** storage, perf
**Parent:** #478 (`SN-WEB-001`)
**Depends on:** #180 (`SN-CORE-004`), `SN-WEB-002` (`SN-WEB-002`)
**Security controls:** `MASVS-STORAGE-1`, `MASVS-CODE-4`, `OWASP-A03`, `CWE-89`, `CWE-400`

> New here? Read `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/README.md` first — they explain the architecture, the security rules, and how issues are structured.

## Context
Local-first means the browser **is** the device store on web (`docs/adr/0010-web-pwa-strategy.md` decision 3). The chosen stack is **drift on SQLite-WASM over OPFS sync access handles inside a Worker**: OPFS (`navigator.storage.getDirectory()` + `createSyncAccessHandle()`, Worker-only) is the performance tier available on Chrome/Edge 86+, Firefox 111+ and Safari 15.2+, IndexedDB is the compatibility fallback, and `localStorage` is for small preferences only — **never** note content (`docs/platform/web.md` §4). Putting the database in a Worker also keeps persistence off the UI thread, which the architecture requires so that a write can never add a millisecond to ink latency (CLAUDE.md §8, `docs/architecture/overview.md` §6). This issue delivers the same `sane_core` repository contract as native, backed by the web store, implementing `PRD-STOR-001` and `PRD-STOR-002` on web.

## Scope
**In:** a web storage backend under `app/lib/platform/web/storage/` wiring drift's web build to SQLite-WASM over OPFS in a dedicated Worker; a content-addressed blob store for ink/PDF/audio payloads in OPFS; an IndexedDB fallback when sync access handles are unavailable; schema creation and migration; a preference store on `localStorage` limited to non-content keys; quota-aware writes.
**Out:** encryption at rest and key handling (`SN-WEB-031`), persistence/eviction UX (`SN-WEB-009`), sync to the user's cloud (`SN-WEB-019`), and the shared schema definition itself (#180).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Creating a notebook, writing 500 strokes across 5 pages, reloading the tab and reopening reproduces the document **byte-for-byte** at the stroke-serialisation level.
- [ ] The database and all blob I/O run in a Worker; a profile capture during continuous writing shows no storage work on the main thread and no frame over 16.7 ms.
- [ ] Opening a 1,000-page notebook completes in **< 1 s** on Chrome desktop (budget parity with native, `docs/platform/performance-budgets.md`).
- [ ] When `createSyncAccessHandle` is unavailable, the IndexedDB fallback engages automatically and all functional tests still pass (slower is acceptable, data loss is not).
- [ ] Every storage call is wrapped so a `QuotaExceededError` produces a typed `Failure` and a user-safe message, never an unhandled exception or a partially written note.
- [ ] Two tabs open on the same origin do not corrupt the database: the second tab either shares the Worker or fails closed with a clear "open in another tab" state.
- [ ] No note content, title or blob is ever written to `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` — asserted by a test that scans both stores after a scripted session.

## Technical notes
Implement the `sane_core` repository interfaces (#178, #180) so `app/` code is unaware of the backend; `packages/sane_core` stays pure Dart with no web import (package DAG, `docs/architecture/overview.md` §5). Use **parameterised queries via drift only** — never string-built SQL (secure-coding checklist §9.1). Content-address blobs with the same hash function as native (#180) so `.sanenote` bundles and sync segments are portable. Keep the Worker's message protocol typed and minimal. Cross-origin isolation is not required for OPFS, but the Worker must keep functioning when it is enabled (`SN-WEB-015`). Implements `PRD-STOR-001`, `PRD-STOR-002`, `PRD-STOR-008` and ADR-0010 decision 3.

## Security & privacy
Threats: SQL injection through any hand-built query (OWASP-A03, CWE-89); unbounded blob writes filling the user's disk or being used as a decompression-bomb landing zone (CWE-400); note content leaking into `localStorage`, which is readable by any script running on the origin and is where an XSS payload would look first (MASVS-STORAGE-1, CWE-312); untrusted data deserialised into arbitrary types (MASVS-CODE-4, CWE-502). Controls: drift parameterised statements everywhere; size caps and a wall-clock timeout before any decode or blob write (checklist §1); OPFS-only for content, `localStorage` restricted to an allow-list of preference keys enforced by a lint-style test; explicit, validated model deserialisation; all failures typed as `Result<T, Failure>` and fail-closed. OPFS is origin-private but is **not** a boundary against local malware — the crypto in `SN-WEB-031` is (ADR-0010 Security impact).

## UX notes
Invisible when healthy, decisive when not. The Library and Editor screens (`docs/design/screens-and-flows.md` §6, §7) must show a skeleton loading state, an empty state for a new workspace, and a clear, non-blaming error state when the store cannot open ("Sane Notes can't open your notes in this browser" with a retry and an export path). All states are tokenised through `sane_ui` so they render in all **17 looks, light and dark**. Accessibility: error and loading states announce via `Semantics` live regions, controls are keyboard reachable with visible focus, 44 px targets, ≥ 4.5:1 contrast.

## Test plan
- `app/test/web/opfs_store_test.dart` — CRUD, migration, quota error mapping, fallback selection (mocked handles).
- `app/test/web/local_storage_allowlist_test.dart` — asserts no content key ever reaches `localStorage`.
- `app/integration_test/web/persistence_roundtrip_test.dart` — headless Chromium: write, reload, verify byte-for-byte; 1,000-page open timing.
- `app/integration_test/web/two_tab_test.dart` — concurrent tab behaviour.
- Manual: Safari iPadOS (sync access handle support), Firefox 125, and a quota-pressure run per `docs/platform/web.md

sample.title: An ADR number is verified, and renumbering is one command
sample.body:
## The problem

An ADR number is claimed by writing a filename, and nothing notices when two
branches claim the same one. It happened three times in one afternoon:
ADR-0081, ADR-0082 and ADR-0089 were each taken by another session between the
moment a branch picked a number and the moment it rebased. Every time the
symptom was the same — a rebase conflict or, worse, two files silently sharing
a number — and the fix was a manual `git mv` plus a hand-audit of every
reference to it in ADRs, skills, `AGENTS.md`, workflow comments and tool source.

Two things are missing:

1. **Nothing detects a duplicate.** `docs/decisions/` could hold two
   `ADR-0089-*.md` files and every check in the repository would pass. The
   filename is the identifier, and it is unvalidated.
2. **Renumbering is manual and easy to get half-right.** An ADR is referenced
   by filename *and* by its heading *and* by prose like "(ADR-0089)". Missing
   one leaves a link that resolves to somebody else's decision, which is worse
   than a broken link because it reads as correct.

The delivery contract already says to rebase before every push. In practice the
collision is created earlier — at the moment the file is named — so the guidance
is one step too late.

## Proposed change

- `tools/adr-numbers.mjs`:
  - `--check` (default) — fail on a duplicate number, on a filename whose
    number disagrees with its heading, and on a malformed name. Wire into the
    `docs` CI job and the pre-commit hook.
  - `--next` — print the next free number, considering `origin/main` **and**
    every fetched remote branch, so a number another open pull request has
    already claimed is skipped rather than collided with.
  - `--renumber <old> <new>` — `git mv` the file and rewrite every reference to
    it across the repository in one command, so losing a race costs a command
    rather than an audit.
- Guidance: rebase onto fresh `origin/main` before **committing**, not only
  before pushing, and take the number after that rebase.
- A lesson under `docs/lessons/`, since this is a real recurring incident, and
  by [ADR-0085](docs/decisions/ADR-0085-a-lesson-flows-upstream-into-the-specification.md)'s
  amendment a process lesson also updates the skill that would have prevented
  it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Two ADRs sharing a number fail the `docs` job and the pre-commit hook.
- An ADR whose filename number and heading number disagree fails.
- `--next` skips a number claimed on any fetched remote branch, not only on
  `origin/main`.
- `--renumber 0089 0091` moves the file and leaves no reference to the old
  number anywhere in the repository.
- The delivery skill says to rebase before committing, and to take the number
  after the rebase.

## Out of scope

- Abandoning sequential numbers for dates or UUIDs. The numbers are cited in
  prose, commit messages and issue history; they are an identifier people read
  aloud, and churning them would break far more than it fixes.
- Reserving numbers centrally, or any mechanism requiring coordination between
  concurrent sessions before work starts.

sample.title: 0.1.0 has never been published to npm, so the five sites that duplicate this kit have nothing to depend on
sample.body:
## The state

`@kingdom-community/community-site-kit` does not exist on npm. Verified 2026-09-06:

| Check | Command / URL | Observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registry | `https://registry.npmjs.org/@kingdom-community%2fcommunity-site-kit` | **HTTP 404** |
| Releases | `gh release list -R kingdom-community/community-site-kit` | empty |
| Tags | `gh api repos/kingdom-community/community-site-kit/tags` | `0` |
| Release runs | `gh run list -R kingdom-community/community-site-kit --workflow release.yml` | **zero runs, ever** |
| Manifest version | `package.json:3` | `0.1.0` |

`.github/workflows/release.yml` is `workflow_dispatch`-only by design, and says so at line 3:

> `# Manual only. Publishing is the owner's call, never a side effect of merging.`

That design is not in question here. What is being recorded is that the deliberate act it waits for has never been performed, and that this is the single thing standing between the kit and every site that wants it.

The repository is otherwise ready. CI on `main` is green (`ci.yml`, run `34021554079`, `c2f7162`, Node 18/20/22 across `typecheck`, `test`, `build`). `package.json` declares `files`, `main`, `types`, `exports`, `publishConfig`, and a `prepublishOnly` build. `README.md:17` already instructs readers to run:

```
npm install @kingdom-community/community-site-kit
```

— a command that fails today with a 404.

## What is waiting on it

Five independent copies of this kit's surface exist across four organisations. None of them can be retired while there is nothing to depend on. Line counts below were measured 2026-09-06 over `components/{TopBar,BottomBar,ColorModeToggleSwitch,ErrorPage,Seo}.tsx`, `utils/{ColorModeContext,colorMode,nav}.ts`, and — where present — `components/{NextLinkComposed,UnavailablePanel}.tsx`, `styles/styles.ts`, `utils/{seo,sitemap}.ts`:

| Site | Duplicated lines |
| --- | --- |
| The private site this kit was extracted from | **911** |
| `Dans-Plugins/dansplugins-dot-com` | **1056** |
| `Preponderous-Software/preponderous-dot-org` | **800** |
| `Preponderous-Software/roam-website` | **609** |
| A second private site elsewhere in the fleet | **737** |

Roughly 4,100 lines of the same five components and three utilities, maintained five times.

An org-wide code search for `"@kingdom-community/" in:file filename:package.json` returns **0 results**. No repository anywhere depends on this package, because no repository can.

### One site has already paid the upgrade cost in advance

`Dans-Plugins/dansplugins-dot-com` upgraded Next.js from 12.2.2 to 14.2.35 specifically to clear this kit's peer floor. Its `CHANGELOG.md:11` states the reason outright:

> "…the floor `@kingdom-community/community-site-kit` requires (`next >= 13`), so the shared component kit that exists to retire this site's duplicated components can now be adopted."

That upgrade — including a real `NextLinkComposed.tsx` fix for the Next 13 anchor change — has landed, and the payoff is blocked on a publish that has not happened.

### Adoption readiness splits cleanly on the Next.js floor

`package.json` declares `"next": ">=13"` in `peerDependencies`. Measured against each site's `package.json`:

- **Ready the moment 0.1.0 is published:** `Dans-Plugins/dansplugins-dot-com` (Next 14.2.35), and the private site this kit was extracted from (also Next 14.2.35).
- **Needs a Next.js upgrade first:** `Preponderous-Software/preponderous-dot-org`, `Preponderous-Software/roam-website`, and the second private site (all on Next 12.2.2).

That suggests the sensible sequencing: publish, adopt in the two sites that already qualify, and treat the remaining three as separate upgrade-then-adopt work rather than as reasons to delay the release.

## What must happen

1. **Confirm the publish credential exists.** `release.yml:36` reads `secrets.NPM_TOKEN`. `gh api repos/kingdom-community/community-site-kit/actions/secrets` reports `total_count: 0`, so no repository-level secret is set — but an organisation-level secret would satisfy the workflow just as well, and organisation secrets could **not** be read from here (`gh api orgs/kingdom-community/actions/secrets` returned **HTTP 403**, "You must be an org admin or have the actions secrets fine-grained permission"). **This is therefore unverified, not a known gap.** Confirmation that `NPM_TOKEN` resolves — and that the npm account owns the `@kingdom-community` scope with publish rights — should happen before the workflow is fired, not after it fails.
2. **Decide whether `0.1.0` is the right first version.** The manifest says `0.1.0` and nothing has ever shipped, so the number is still free. If the intent is to signal an unstable API while the five sites migrate, `0.1.0` is right as it stands; if the intent is to signal that the surface is settled, it should be bumped before the first publish rather than after consumers have pinned it.
3. **Fire `release.yml` from `main`.** It re-runs `typecheck`, `test` and `build` before publishing, and publishes with `--provenance --access public`. The `tag` input defaults to `latest`.
4. **Unblock the consumer issues.** Once the package resolves, the two Next 14 sites can each replace their copies with a dependency.

## Open questions

- **Is green CI sufficient to release?** CI covers `typecheck`, `test` and `build` on Node 18, 20 and 22, but nothing has ever exercised the packed tarball — `files`, the `exports` map, and the `dist/` layout have never been validated by an actual install. Unlike this org's `session-client` release workflow, `release.yml` here has no `dry_run` input, so there is no way to run `npm pack` through it without publishing. A local `npm pack` and an install of the resulting tarball into one of the five sites would settle whether the package shape is correct before it is permanent — npm versions cannot be re-published once taken.
- **Should the first publish carry a non-`latest` dist-tag?** The workflow accepts a `tag` input. Publishing `0.1.0` under `next` first wo

sample.title: Confirm supported large native image messages without exhausting history reads
sample.body:
Part of the native attachment requirement in #1647 and the native parity work in #1629.

A credential-free integration with real Codex 0.154 accepts, edits and starts a queued message containing four readable 3 MiB PNG files (16 MiB base64 in total). The local Responses fixture receives the image turn, but the Viewer entry remains `dispatching`. Its canonical reader returns `unknown/bytes`: the default 16 MiB aggregate history budget is smaller than the accepted image input plus its JSON envelope. The equivalent small-image control passes. Requesting full turn pages in #1661 fixes excessive per-turn RPCs but does not fix this byte-budget mismatch.

Repair confirmation for supported large inputs using exact canonical client, thread, turn, content and attachment evidence. Keep bounded reads and safe unknown outcomes; avoid rescanning the complete historical conversation for every positive acknowledgement. Match the accepted payload contract and ensure that multiple queued image messages cannot overflow the host response-frame handling. This backend work must coordinate with the browser durability changes in #1652.

Acceptance: real native queue add/edit/start and ordinary delivery with four large images, correct canonical receipts, no duplicate resend after a lost acknowledgement/reload/cold recovery, retained payloads when evidence is missing or conflicting, and responsive small control operations. Use isolated local Responses fixtures without account credentials or live user state. Include the reproduced large-input failure as the causal baseline.

sample.title: The pages guest is stale on dev: its component.wasm does not match a rebuild of its source
sample.body:
`make wasm-rebuild-check` is red on plain `dev`, at ee0c479d1, in a clean detached worktree with no branch's changes in it:

```
crates/modules/apps/pages/component.wasm .../target/wasm-rebuild-check/pages.component.wasm differ: byte 1270, line 13
crates/modules/apps/pages/component.wasm does not match a rebuild of its source.
```

`inbox` and `files` are checked before it and match, so this is one guest, not the whole sweep. The check stops at the first mismatch, so there may be more behind it.

**It is not a toolchain difference.** This box runs `rustc 1.96.1 (31fca3adb 2026-06-26)`, which is exactly what `rust-toolchain.toml` pins and what the committed bytes carry in their panic paths.

**It is not a change to pages' own source.** `crates/modules/apps/pages/component.wasm` and its `guest.lock` were last written by 8dded15d6 (#2216), and nothing under `crates/modules/apps/pages` has changed since.

**It is a dependency of the guest that moved without pages being rebuilt** — the case AGENTS.md now names (#2379). Two commits touched a crate the pages guest compiles in, after that rebuild:

- `51105ee30 fix(files): put the object-read cap where a guest dispatch can reach it` — pages links `files = { path = "../files", default-features = false }`. `files`' own component.wasm WAS refreshed, which is why it passes the check and pages does not.
- `b32fb56e1 perf(runs): move the tenant onto its store so a block stops carrying the receipt history (#2333)`.

The fix is the one the check prints:

```
cargo run -p guest-builder -- crates/modules/apps/pages
```

committed with its kernel fixture copy. Whoever refreshes it should run the whole `make wasm-rebuild-check` afterwards rather than stopping at pages, since the check exits at the first mismatch and a second stale guest would still be hiding behind this one.

Note for anyone reproducing: `guest-builder` bakes its platform root at compile time, so on a shared Cargo target it may be another worktree's binary and refuses with "`crates/modules/apps/pages` is outside the platform checkout <other worktree>". `touch bin/guest-builder/src/main.rs` and rebuild first.

sample.title: Add immutable dct:creator in <doc>.meta Resource
sample.body:
## Design: immutable `dct:creator` in `.meta` (per-document provenance)

### Goal
Give every plain document a server-enforced, immutable `dct:creator`, declared by the client **before** the document exists, then locked for the document's lifetime.

### Scope
- **Target:** plain documents only — non-container, non-auxiliary resources.
- **Location:** the creator triple lives in the document's `.meta`:
  `<doc> dct:creator <webId>` (`http://purl.org/dc/terms/creator`)
- **Excluded:** containers; auxiliary resources (`.acl`, `.meta`) as subjects.
- **Precedent:** pod root already carries a server-owned `<./> a space:Storage` triple.

### Lifecycle & method matrix

**Declaration — document does not exist:**
| Method | Target | Allowed? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| PUT | `<doc>.meta` | ✅ | The only declaration channel; client sets `dct:creator`. *Needs change: today PUT on any `.meta` is blanket-rejected.* |
| POST | (would mint a `.meta`-named child) | ❌ | Containers must never create auxiliary docs. *Explicit new rule.* |
| PATCH | `<doc>.meta` | ❌ | Resource absent → 404 (unchanged). |

**Document exists:**
| Method | Target | Allowed? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| PUT / POST | `<doc>` | ✅ | Existing `.meta` (incl. `dct:creator`) must be **preserved** (write-once). |
| PUT | `<doc>.meta` | ❌ | Current rule unchanged. |
| PATCH | `<doc>.meta` | ✅ (except creator) | Other metadata editable; `dct:creator` immutable → 409 on change/removal. |
| DELETE | `<doc>` | ✅ | Doc + `.meta` removed together; creator dies with it. |
| DELETE | `<doc>.meta` alone | ❌ | Surgical provenance removal — forbidden. |
| GET | `<doc>.meta` | ✅ | Creator readable. |

**No declaration happened?** → document is created without `dct:creator` (absent, never forged). Agent-derived default (option A) is a possible future extension, not part of this.

### Enforcement pieces
1. **PATCH immutability** — add a `dct:creator` `FilterPattern` to `ImmutableMetadataPatcher` (`patching.json`) → *config-only*.
2. **Declaration channel** — `PutOperationHandler`: allow PUT on `.meta` **only when the subject document is absent** (currently rejects before checking existence) + reject container POSTs that would mint `.meta`-named children.
3. **Preservation** — document creation/overwrite must not clobber a pre-existing `.meta` `dct:creator` (store-level, reusing the `solid-meta:preserve` mechanism).
4. **Delete protection** — DELETE targeting only the `.meta` of an existing document → 403/409.

### Open implementation checks (for the issue)
- How `DataAccessorBasedStore.setRepresentation` behaves for a `.meta` identifier whose subject doesn't exist yet.
- Slug/POST validation to block `.meta`-named child creation.
- Subject IRI / `baseIRI` of the `dct:creator` triple inside the serialized `.meta`.

sample.title: Flaky under load — the two acceptance tests that spawn ESLint run against vitest's 5s default timeout
sample.body:
## Symptom

`apps/react/src/acceptance/criterion-06-cycle.test.ts` and `criterion-08-lint-preset.test.ts` hit
vitest's **5 s default timeout** when the machine is busy. Observed during #62's doc work with four
agents running concurrently; both pass in isolation, and repeatedly.

This is not a race in the tests. Both spawn **ESLint in a subprocess** — that is the point of them,
since they prove the lint half of criteria 6 and 8 against real files through the real root config
— and an ESLint run that takes ~1 s idle takes far longer on a loaded machine.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than shrugging at

A test whose duration is dominated by a subprocess, running under a timeout chosen for in-memory
unit tests, will fail on a busy CI runner. When it does, it will look like a defect in the boundary
rules — the loudest, most alarming possible false positive, on exactly the tests that exist to
prove the boundary rules work.

There is precedent here for treating this shape seriously: a demo test that "passed almost always"
turned out never to have been guarded at all, and the fix was to make the wait explicit rather than
to accept the flake.

## Fix

Give the subprocess-spawning tests a timeout that reflects what they do, rather than raising the
global default — a slow *unit* test should still fail fast. Per-test `{ timeout: … }` on the two
tests, or a small named constant shared by both with a comment saying why it is not the default.

While there: check whether anything else in the workspace shells out inside a test
(`packages/eslint-config-modules/src/no-cycle.test.ts` runs ESLint in-process via the API, which is
a different cost profile — confirm rather than assume).

## Done when

- Both tests carry an explicit, justified timeout and the global default is unchanged.
- Evidence they survive load: run the suite under contention (a handful of CPU burners, or in
  parallel with a full `pnpm verify`) enough times to mean something, and report the numbers before
  and after. `vitest run --repeat=N` does **not** exist in Vitest 4 — use a shell loop.
- A sweep result for other tests that spawn processes, with a verdict per test rather than only the
  ones changed.

Found during #62 (PR #64), where it was correctly identified as unrelated to the change under review.

sample.title: NetGrip-managed agent gone stale has no recovery path in the UI
sample.body:
## Summary

A router whose agent is the embedded NetGrip one (`kind=netgrip`) can end up **stale (inactive)** with **no recovery action available** in the fleet UI, even when the operator has working SSH to the router. The only actions that exist for netgrip agents are blocked by design (#363), and the one that would recover it (Update) only appears when `updateAvailable` is true.

## Repro / scenario (real production case)

- Router runs NetGrip with its embedded agent (no standalone `netpulse-agent`).
- The NetGrip process was started **before** the agent token was rotated / `/etc/netgrip/netpulse.env` was rewritten, so the running process keeps the **old token in memory**. The on-disk env matches the server hash, but every ingest push fails with `HTTP 401` (`buffered=100 dropped=57x` in router logs), so the server marks the agent stale for as long as the process is not restarted.
- In the fleet UI the row shows **Inactive** with the hint "The agent lives in the NetGrip panel", but:
  - **Rearm** and **Reinstall** are intentionally hidden for `kind=netgrip` (would deploy the standalone binary over NetGrip and break it, #363).
  - **Update** only renders when `updateAvailable` is true (older version available).
  - Result: if the NetGrip panel is already on the latest version (or the check has not flagged it), there is **no button and no guidance** telling the operator to restart the NetGrip service on the router. The agent looks unrecoverable from NetPulse.

Recovery that works today (undocumented in the UI): restart NetGrip on the router (`/etc/init.d/netgrip stop && start`, note `restart` can be a no-op) or trigger the panel self-update via the Update button when available. Either reloads the env and the agent comes back fresh.

## Suggestion

1. For a stale `netgrip` agent, surface an actionable hint or action that explains the recovery path (restart the NetGrip service on the router / panel self-update), instead of only "the agent lives in the NetGrip panel".
2. Optionally expose the raw ingest error (e.g. the `401`) in the agent row/tooltip so a stale agent caused by an old in-memory token is diagnosable without router logs.

## Notes

- Server/UI behavior verified against the current code paths (`handleAgentRearm`/`handleAgentReinstall` return `409 netgrip_managed` for netgrip; `AgentRow` renders the netgrip hint and only Update is offered).
- Distinct from #564/#566/#567 (fresh-install SSH discovery flow of another user); this is about an already-managed NetGrip agent going stale.

sample.title: Expose canonical agent authoring operations to onboarding
sample.body:
**Reviewed handoff — implement after the listed prerequisites have been verified.**

**Scope:** `cross-workspace` · **Size:** L · **Effort:** 8/10

Grounded against [monorepo 2932448711de](https://github.com/FlyCockpit/flycockpitapp/tree/2932448711de3984c1a1fef21dda662b5219f7c9); reference UI snapshot `55bedc0bd4586f86a8ae2df7cafcfe72bb522cbf`.

## Prerequisites

- #388

Related implemented contracts: #78, #242.

Batch tracking and shared coverage: #404.

## Goal

Let onboarding create a real authored agent with multiple model grants and a
default, explicit model trust, optimization/self-verification settings, tool
tiers, nested subagents, and a reviewable creation plan—by using the canonical
agent-definition, installation, and daemon mutation authorities already in the
product.

## Current behavior

- The current onboarding plan is a catalog installer. `OnboardingAgentAnswers`
  and `OnboardingAgentPlan` carry one model, one model-trust choice, tool
  selection, sidecar choice, and default flag
  (`crates/cockpit-core/src/onboarding_agent.rs:74-124,157-264`), and its
  descriptor is titled “Install your coding agent”
  (`crates/cockpit-core/src/wizard/mod.rs:659-961`).
- `AgentDef` is already the runtime definition (`crates/cockpit-core/src/agents/mod.rs:309-412`).
  Its launch-v1 frontmatter is the canonical closed schema
  (`:1518-1611`): `ModelSlot.models` represents allowed models plus a default
  (`crates/cockpit-core/src/agents/vnext.rs:1723-1810`),
  `toolTierPreferences` is canonical, and private subagents are explicit.
  Verification and delegation live in the same frontmatter contract.
- Model trust is presently a global provider/model configuration value, with
  explicit confirmation in onboarding (`onboarding_agent.rs:5-31,157-180`),
  not an onboarding-only security bypass. The current plan writes that existing
  model configuration (`:103-124`).
- Installed-agent binding, provider-route resolution, journals, and default
  selection already belong to `daemon/agent_installation.rs:1-46` and the
  squashed schema's `agent_default_installation`/
  `onboarding_agent_publication_journals` tables
  (`crates/cockpit-db/src/db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:8014-8154`).
  General agent mutations have revision and durable settlement semantics
  (`crates/cockpit-proto/src/agent_management.rs:101-198`;
  `crates/cockpit-core/src/daemon/agent_management.rs:4386-4391`).

## Root cause

The onboarding descriptor/projector was created for installing a catalog item,
while canonical authoring evolved elsewhere. Extending its local answer/plan
types would create a second agent schema and bypass the existing installation,
publication, and replay authorities.

## Desired behavior

Create an onboarding-facing, renderer-independent authoring projection and
apply/reconcile operations that project to canonical `AgentDef` frontmatter and
existing installation/default authorities. It supports authored first-party and
pinned third-party sources; no onboarding path invents a provider model,
pretends a capability exists, or downgrades any trust/egress confirmation.
The source chooser retains the actual bundled frontier agent as the offline
first-run safety net and real, configured-model-filtered first-party catalog
entries when online; authoring changes the canonical selected definition rather
than replacing source/installation semantics.

## Decisions made

- Reuse canonical fields where they already exist: `modelSlots.*.models` plus
  its one default for model grants; `toolTierPreferences` for author
  preferences; `delegation` and package private subagents for nesting;
  `verification` for self-verification; existing provider/model `trust` for
  per-selected-model custody; and the existing sidecar/remote-egress gate.
- Closed GitHub #78 established load-bearing multi-model `AgentDef` slots and
  closed #242 established agent installation/default selection. Treat both as
  already canonical. Reuse existing authorities where they exist; for a
  reference control without one, add the clean v1 canonical frontmatter/runtime
  field specified by this issue, with no shadow JSON, onboarding-only format,
  compatibility alias, or local-only setting.
- “Per-agent trust” means an explicit trust confirmation and durable trust
  classification for every model grant the new agent can select. The model
  configuration remains the policy authority. If a single model is used by two
  agents, the UI must disclose that its custody classification is shared rather
  than silently claiming independent policy.
- Third-party sources retain canonical source parsing, pinned revision, content
  validation, and publisher confirmation. Built-in/default authoring uses the
  same `AgentDef` validation and installation result path, never a mock catalog
  object.
- The bundled frontier agent remains usable offline with configured compatible
  providers. Online catalog entries are filtered by actual configured model
  capabilities; an unavailable network/catalog uses its existing cached/bundled
  path rather than inventing a generic default model.
- Create/default/review operations are daemon-owned, CAS/idempotency-bound,
  and registered with the onboarding authority from the prerequisite prompt.
  Unknown settlement is queried by its exact operation; it is never retried as
  a fresh create.
- No compatibility aliases or old catalog-installer descriptor remain. Replace
  `OnboardingAgentAnswers`, `OnboardingAgentPlan`, and their descriptor/apply
  path when the new projection reaches parity; retain only generic non-first-run
  agent-install commands that have distinct, documented purpose.

## Edge cases and UX decisions

- At least one model grant is required and exactly one enabled model is the
  default. The default cannot be removed until another grant is selected.
- Each grant must resolve against the real configured provider catalog and its
  capabilities. Missing/changed provider routes or capability generation makes
  review st

sample.title: [E07-F03-4] The cross-branch transfer grant and the overdue-transfer sweep
sample.body:
Sub-issue of #37. Two things the transfer needs and E07-F03-2 deliberately left out. The first is the one
sanctioned exception to branch isolation in the whole system: `docs/prd/workflows/branch-scenarios.md` **BR-8** —
"The one narrow exception to BR-3 is `TransferScopeRequirement`: while a cross-branch custody transfer is pending,
users of the destination branch holding `custody.receive` may perform exactly the receive, reject and resolve
actions on the listed jobs, and nothing else | Issue #37" — and `docs/adr/0007-branch-aware-single-tenancy.md`
line 249 assigns its tests here by name. The second is the expiry clock: `custody.custody-transfer-overdue.v1` is
a published event name in `docs/architecture/module-ownership.md` section 5.6 with nothing raising it. Neither
exists: `grep -rn "TransferScope" src/` returns **nothing**, and `src/Hosts/Tailor360.Worker/Jobs/` holds six jobs
and none of them is a custody sweep.

## What is already built (do not re-build)

- **E07-F03-2** (merge first) — `custody.custody_transfers` with `from_branch_id`, `to_branch_id`, `expires_at`
  written **null**, its `pending`→terminal trigger, `CustodyResourceKinds.Transfer` and
  `CustodyTransferScopeResolver`, which returns the transfer's **owning** branch and therefore refuses a
  destination-branch caller today. This slice is what admits them, narrowly.
- **E07-F03-3** (merge first) — `custody.reconciliation_cases` and the rejected-transfer arm, so an expiry has a
  case to open (`docs/prd/state-transitions.md` section 4.1 line 287: "Transfer pending → Reject or expire →
  Reconciliation case open"). **E07-F03-3b** (merge first) — `POST /custody/cases/{caseId}/corrections`, the
  "resolve" action BR-8 names and the third route this slice decorates.
- `src/Platform/Tailor360.Platform.Security/Authorisation/` — `ResourceScope` (Kind, ResourceId, **one**
  `BranchId`, `AssignedUserIds`), `IResourceScopeResolver`, `ResourceScopeStatus` with its `Unresolved = 0` that
  "is a refusal, not a pass", and `ResourceOwnershipRequirement` as the worked example of a requirement that reads
  the resolved scope. **`ResourceScope` carries exactly one branch**, which is why the cross-branch grant cannot
  be smuggled through a resolver and needs its own requirement — say so in the pull request.
- `src/Hosts/Tailor360.Worker/Jobs/DispatchExceptionExpiryService.cs` — the worker idiom to copy line for line:
  `[WorkerJob(JobName, WorkerBranchScope.None)]` (ARCH-021), `IWorkerScopeFactory` (ARCH-020), a named lease, a
  fixed `BatchSize`, a `RunInterval`, and a remark explaining why a missed pass is harmless.
- `src/Platform/Tailor360.Platform.Security/Background/WorkerJobAttribute.cs`, `WorkerJobDescriptor.cs` and
  `IWorkerScopeFactory.cs` — a job with no `[WorkerJob]` is refused its scope, by design.
- `src/Modules/Identity/Tailor360.Modules.Identity.Contracts/Directory/IBranchDirectory.cs` — `BranchSummary` with
  `Code`, `Name`, `TimeZoneId`: the only lawful source of the branch timezone an expiry instant is computed in
  (ARCH-014 forbids `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow`; use `IClock`).
- `src/Platform/Tailor360.Platform.Security/Permissions/CustodyPermissions.cs` — `Receive`, `RejectTransfer`,
  `Reconcile`; all three already granted and already in `docs/security/permission-matrix.md`. **No new permission
  key**: the grant this slice adds is a *reach*, not a permission.

## Scope

- [ ] **`TransferScopeRequirement`** in `src/Platform/Tailor360.Platform.Security/Authorisation/`, with its
      authorisation handler, admitting a caller who (a) holds the endpoint's permission, (b) is assigned to the
      transfer's `to_branch_id`, and (c) names a transfer that is **still `pending`** — and admitting them for
      **exactly** the receive, reject and resolve actions on that transfer's jobs and nothing else (INV-CDY-04,
      BR-8). The grant ends the moment the transfer is accepted, rejected or expired; it is re-evaluated per
      request and never cached beyond it.
- [ ] **`ITransferGrantSource`** beside it — a platform port (`CLAUDE.md` section 3 mechanism 5) the requirement
      asks, because the platform never queries a module's tables (the rule `IResourceScopeResolver`'s own remarks
      state). It answers identifiers only: the transfer's state, its `to_branch_id` and its job set. Implemented
      by `Custody.Infrastructure` as one indexed read and registered in `AddCustodyModule`.
- [ ] **Apply it to exactly three routes**, by adding `.WithinPendingTransferScope()` beside the existing
      `.RequirePermission(...)` on E07-F03-2's receive (`POST /custody/transfers/{transferId}/receive`) and reject
      (`…/reject`), and on **E07-F03-3b's** correction route (`POST /custody/cases/{caseId}/corrections`) — which is
      what BR-8's "resolve" means and is why **E07-F03-3b, not E07-F03-3, is the dependency**: E07-F03-3 has no
      correction route to decorate. The case **approval** is deliberately left out, so a destination-branch user may
      propose the repair and never sign it off. The
      ordinary branch-scope check remains and the new requirement **widens nothing else**: the transfer-out route,
      the case approval, the queue reads and every other custody route keep plain branch scope.
- [ ] **After acceptance, custody moves branch.** `job_custody_state.current_custody_branch_id` becomes the
      destination on accept, so ordinary branch scope then admits the destination and excludes the origin for
      custody actions — while order and billing ownership stay with the originating branch, which this slice never
      touches (plan Section 8, #37, "Cross-branch transfers").
- [ ] **`CustodyTransferSlaOptions`** bound to `Custody:TransferSla`, a map of transfer type to duration plus a
      `PolicyVersion`, with an `IValidateOptions<>` validator. **Default: empty.** An unconfigured transfer type
      gets `expires_at = null` and never goes overdue and never expires, because **FBH-03** says in terms "No
      nu

sample.title: distribution: Smithery still says "four-axis score", and two directories remain unsubmitted
sample.body:
Maintainer-side follow-ups from the distribution audit in PR #466. All three need a login or a form, so none can be done from the repo.

## 1. Smithery description is stale (the actionable one)

https://smithery.ai/skills/alex-1c6e/archy currently reads:

> Track architectural health of a Python codebase via the archy CLI and MCP server. Computes a **four-axis** quality score (modularity, acyclic...

The score has **five** axes: modularity, acyclicity, depth, equality, complexity. The listing predates the complexity axis. Confirmed against `skills/archy/SKILL.md` and the submission kit in `docs/MCP_DIRECTORIES.md`, which both say five.

Copy to paste, from the kit (already current, 13 tools):

> Python architecture analysis: import graph, cycles, layer rules, five-axis score, refactor-priority hotspots, DSM, and an MCP server (13 tools) so coding agents see structural impact before they commit.

While logged in, worth checking the rest of the listing against the kit in the same pass, since nothing else has verified it since submission.

## 2. mcp.so: still unlisted

https://mcp.so/submit is form-based and asks for submitter identity. `https://mcp.so/server/archy` returns 404, so archy is genuinely absent rather than listed under another slug (worth a search on the site to be sure, since the URL shape was a guess).

## 3. PulseMCP: cannot verify from here

https://www.pulsemcp.com/servers?q=archy returns **403** to a scripted request, so whether archy is listed is unknown. Check it in a browser before submitting, so a duplicate submission is not filed.

## Why these are worth a few minutes

From the usage research on 2026-09-05: discovery is almost entirely passive (Google was 142 of 168 unique visitors in 14 days), and real usage is fewer than 20 people. Directory listings are one of the few channels that work without ongoing effort, and the one channel that was measurably broken (#462) had been broken for three weeks with nobody noticing.

The counterweight, worth stating: a stale axis count is not why archy has few users, and submitting to two more directories is not a growth strategy. These are cheap correctness fixes on channels that already exist, not a plan.

- #462, the registry entry that was broken and stale
