sample.title: [Bug]: kanban respawn guard does not cover repeated clean-exit-without-transition — 16 consecutive respawns on one card
sample.body:
## Summary

The respawn guard (`respawn_guarded`: `blocker_auth`, `recent_success`, `active_pr`, `rate_limit_cooldown`) does not cover the most common recurring failure we see: a worker that starts, runs ~2-4 minutes, exits `rc=0` without any board transition, and is then re-spawned by the same wave logic. On our board that pattern repeated **16+ consecutive runs on one card** before a human intervened, burning provider tokens on every pass and never tripping `failure_limit`/auto-block.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.21.3 (2026.9.14) git install; SQLite 3.46.1 (`journal_mode=delete`)
- `kanban.dispatch_in_gateway=false`; a systemd timer runs `hermes kanban dispatch --max 5` every 90s; `failure_limit` default (2)
- All work cards `goal_mode=1`, `goal_max_turns=60` (set specifically to stop clean-exit deaths)

## Evidence

```
-- t_420e60b7: runs 38,40,42,44,47,49,51,53,55,57,59,61,63,65,67 → 15 consecutive runs
   each ~92-137s, each closed with
   err='manual_reclaim: sequencer: stale run (dead worker)'

-- t_f92bd699: runs 37,39,41,43,45,48,50,52,54,56,58,60,62,64,66,68 → 16 consecutive runs
   each ~203-266s, same close reason

-- same board: run 5 on t_f92bd699 got the honest classification
   err='worker exited cleanly (rc=0) without calling kanban_complete'
   → and was still respawned on later ticks
```

Event counts board-wide: `spawned 53`, `claimed 53`, `reclaimed 29`, `respawn_guarded 17`, `crashed 4`, `protocol_violation 4`, `gave_up 1`.

The guard that did fire was for other reasons (`blocker_auth`, `rate_limit_cooldown`), never for this class. Because a clean exit is not a "failure" as far as `consecutive_failures` is concerned, the auto-block breaker never trips and the loop is unbounded — our automation only stopped it because it happens to reclaim stale runs itself and the operator watched the board.

## Suggested direction

Treat "clean exit with no terminal transition" as a first-class failure for the circuit breaker: increment the same counter used by `failure_limit`, and after N consecutive occurrences of the same class on a card, block it (`blocked` with a distinct reason, e.g. `no-terminal-transition`) instead of re-spawning. Right now the only defense is operator tooling outside the dispatcher, which every board owner would have to reimplement.

## Related observation (may belong in a separate report)

The same wave shows startup-phase deaths that look different in the logs but end the same way: a session footer with `Messages: 1 (1 user, 0 tool calls)` (`Duration: 3s`) and a `rate_limited` outcome recorded 60s later (`pid … exited rate-limited (quota wall) — requeued without claiming`), plus logs that end mid-render with a truncated banner and no footer. Worker stderr/stdout tails are truncated in the run row (`worker_output`), which makes provider-quota vs. genuine startup crash hard to tell apart after the fact.

sample.title: [P2] Bind deterministic agent stages to verified source functions and execute one typed lifecycle
sample.body:
**Audit:** 2026-09-05, commit [`2b3b1ee24da2`](https://github.com/wavect/semaprax/commit/2b3b1ee24da260ad5407f84b8a292a44dbf47964).
**Classification:** Documented core-agent integration gap; proposed bounded language feature. **Priority:** P2.

## Finding

AgentDefinition currently records identities for `initialize`, `observe`, `authorize`, and `reduce`, but does not execute those declarations as Semaprax functions. The owning specification says so explicitly: [docs/LANGUAGE-NATIVE-AGENT-OBJECT-V1.md](https://github.com/wavect/semaprax/blob/2b3b1ee24da260ad5407f84b8a292a44dbf47964/docs/LANGUAGE-NATIVE-AGENT-OBJECT-V1.md#L36-L56) and [docs/LANGUAGE-NATIVE-AGENT-OBJECT-V1.md](https://github.com/wavect/semaprax/blob/2b3b1ee24da260ad5407f84b8a292a44dbf47964/docs/LANGUAGE-NATIVE-AGENT-OBJECT-V1.md#L282-L301). [src/agent_harness.rs](https://github.com/wavect/semaprax/blob/2b3b1ee24da260ad5407f84b8a292a44dbf47964/src/agent_harness.rs) composes existing runtime/payment kernels and likewise disclaims language-level transition execution.

The result is a useful graph/profile bridge, but the semantic program and harness still do not derive operational behavior from one checked source object.

## First implementation boundary

After proposal grammar and deployment binding are defined, compile a single acyclic lifecycle whose deterministic stage IDs resolve to actual verified `.spx` functions. Start with scalar/closed-record task, state, observation, proposal, outcome, and result types. Validate the stage signatures, ownership modes, effects, and graph edges from the same HIR used for ordinary execution.

Execute the deterministic stages with a retained interpreter product and a scripted model proposal. Limit `execute` initially to one explicitly injected read operation or an effect-free fixture. The authorizing transition must produce an opaque, one-use authorization value bound to the exact proposal/state/policy, not a boolean or hash that any caller can manufacture.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Changing a stage's source changes the compiled agent semantics and invalidates old graph/run bindings.
- [ ] Unresolved IDs, incompatible signatures, incorrect ownership, undeclared effects, stale proposals, and substituted states reject before host work.
- [ ] Only the validated authorize stage can construct the one-use authorization value; reduce/observe/model output cannot.
- [ ] Success, rejection, model failure, effect failure, cancellation, and budget exhaustion have deterministic state/cleanup/evidence behavior.
- [ ] One offline end-to-end example proves task → initialize → observe → propose → authorize → execute → reduce → result.
- [ ] Runtime v1 compatibility bytes and APIs remain frozen.
- [ ] Source remains the Git/review authority; descriptive AgentGraph JSON carries no ambient execution or publication capability.

Keep syntax minimal and versioned; a binding document referencing existing declarations can precede a new `agent` syntax. Durable resume is dependent work, not an implicit property of this lifecycle.

## Agent handoff

Recheck the working revision and existing issues first. Read `AGENTS.md`, the relevant completion-matrix row, and the owning versioned specifications. This proposed slice must preserve canonical source, independent replay, precise target admission, and separately granted authority. Place regressions in the existing owning harness. Execute the applicable quality gates and record what actually ran; unrun native, hosted, or device evidence must stay unpromoted.

## Audit revision scope

Runtime observations in this ticket belong to commit 2b3b1ee24da260ad5407f84b8a292a44dbf47964. A final source-tree comparison against e1c5b56226784c832c63b605e40d1191653e4931 was used to check for obvious superseding changes. That later snapshot was not rebuilt or exhaustively retested. Reproduce on the intended fixing revision before implementation.

**Audit ID:** SPX-AUDIT-20260905-21

**Suggested scope:** L. **Dependencies:** SPX-AUDIT-20260905-17, SPX-AUDIT-20260905-18.

sample.title: Serialize a file-fallback grant write against a daemon start
sample.body:
Follow-up from #182, where this was answered rather than fixed — [the thread](https://github.com/stratuslabs/agent/pull/182#discussion_r4012912667).

## What happens

`stratus grants revoke` writes the grant file directly when it cannot reach a control API. A daemon that reads that agent's grants between the revoke deciding what the file should say and the bytes landing caches the pre-revocation list, and honours the revoked grant until it restarts — after the CLI has reported the revoke as done.

A grant that outlives its revocation is the ratchet the standing-grant work exists to prevent, which is why this is worth closing even though the window is small.

## What it is not

Not something #182 introduced, and worth being precise about, because it was raised there as a migration bug. On `main` before that PR, `save` is `await mkdir(...)` then `await writeFile(...)` — a daemon reading in *that* window caches the same stale grants with no rename anywhere near it. The per-agent move does not widen it either: the open handle follows the inode into the file the new daemon reads.

The underlying property is the store's per-process cache, already documented at `packages/cli/src/commands/grants.ts` (see the class comment, and the warning that "a daemon that is running will not notice until it restarts").

## Why it needs more than a careful write

Closing it means serializing a grant write against a daemon start, across processes. `@stratusagent/state` and `@stratusagent/permissions` have no primitive for that today.

One exists in the right shape: `claimAt` in `packages/gateway/src/lock.ts` — SQLite's own file lock, atomic across processes, never stale (it dies with the descriptor), and with a documented rationale for why a pid file cannot do the job. It is not reusable where it is: `gateway` depends on `state`, not the other way round.

Suggested shape, which is the move CLAUDE.md already prescribes for a private rule that gains a second consumer:

- lift the mechanism into `state` as a lock parameterized by path, with an option to wait rather than fail fast (the home claim wants fail-fast; a short write lock wants to wait);
- `claimHome` becomes a thin policy over it and stays exported from `gateway`, so no importer breaks;
- the grant write takes a lock of its own — **not** the home lock, which the daemon holds for its whole life;
- keep the critical section synchronous, so a second in-process caller cannot block the thread that holds it.

## The contract question this opens

Worth deciding before writing code: what should `stratus grants revoke` do when the home is claimed but the control API is unreachable?

Refusing is not obviously right — today the file write at least makes the grant gone at the next restart, and refusing would leave the operator no way to revoke at all. Whatever is chosen needs a line in `docs/guides/approvals.md`.

## Not needed for the state stamp

Recorded because the same lock was proposed for it during review: the stamp's concurrent-write race was closed in #182 by a different route — one write per run, at the end, carrying the full set, and no write at all from a run that defers an exclusive migration. Every writer now writes the same bytes, so there is nothing left for a lock to protect there.

sample.title: Seven of the eleven inputs score.rb reads are 2-5 days stale, one is watched by nothing, and the tag layer's input is outside the watch list entirely
sample.body:
Four times today a defect turned out to be the same thing: **a derived input that feeds scoring, with nothing scheduling it and — in two cases — nothing watching it either.** Filing the inventory rather than the fifth instance.

## What the scorer actually reads

`score.rb` loads 11 derived JSON inputs. Ages at 2026-09-04, hours before a full `--write`:

```
input                        age   watched by check-stamp-freshness
reversibility.json            0h   yes
applicability.json            5h   yes
mcp-deployment.json            1d  yes
lifecycle.json                 2d  yes      <- stale
needs-work.json                3d  yes      <- stale
pointer-liveness.json          3d  yes      <- stale
agent-card-subject.json        5d  yes      <- stale
alt-contracts.json             5d  yes      <- stale
llms-provenance.json           5d  yes      <- stale
open-source-surface.json       5d  yes      <- stale
webmcp-deployment.json         1d  NO
```

Seven are two to five days behind a catalog whose provider pages are rewritten nightly.

## The four instances behind this

**1. A producer that did not exist.** `domain_standard_conformance` (4 pts) reads `applicability(slug).domain_standards`. 164 providers carried the key and **no committed code produced it**, while `derive-applicability.py` — which owns that file — rebuilds it from an empty dict. The next routine run would have zeroed the check for all 164, silently. Rebuilt and merged today (roadmap#81).

**2. A producer nothing schedules or watches.** `webmcp-deployment.json` grades **730 providers** and feeds the rubric's `webmcp` probe signal. `signals/probe_webmcp.py` writes it, and that script appears in neither `nightly.sh` nor `check-stamp-freshness.py`'s `STAMPS`. It is the only one of the 11 with no freshness check at all.

**3. A whole layer frozen for four days.** `score_tags.rb` writes `signals/_data/tags.json`, which is **not in the 11 and not in STAMPS**. It last ran 2026-08-31. All 15,017 tag pages are frozen at that date — rosters, `provider_count`, `axis`, `facets`, bands — while `group_tags.py` runs nightly against it. `build.py:4835` says so outright: *"which nothing schedules — so the two inputs drift independently and the script reports the skew rather than grouping over it."* Detail on roadmap#263.

**4. An online stamp that can never self-refresh.** `pointer-liveness.json` is watched, but `check-stamp-freshness.py` only regenerates *offline* stamps — an online one probes hosts and is skipped. So it is watched in name and never refreshed in practice. Its fix for roadmap#262 is committed and inert for exactly this reason.

## The shape

`check-stamp-freshness.py` is a good mechanism and its docstring is honest about being **reported, not blocking**. That is the right call for a 40-minute check. But "reported, not blocking" plus a log nobody reads is how four days pass, and the inventory it watches is not the inventory the scorer reads — two inputs are outside it entirely.

## Suggested, cheapest first

1. **Add `webmcp-deployment.json` and `tags.json` to `STAMPS`.** They are scored inputs; the check should know they exist. One-line each.
2. **Schedule `score_tags.rb`** in `nightly.sh` before `group_tags.py`, so the tag layer stops drifting from the catalog it describes.
3. **Make age visible in the scoring output, not only in a log.** The pattern already exists — the coverage block discloses `catalog_gap` rather than hiding it. A scored run that reads a five-day-old input could say so on the record it stamps.
4. **Derive the watched list from what the scorer reads**, rather than maintaining it by hand. `score.rb`'s inputs are greppable; a drift between the two lists is exactly what let (2) and (3) through.

Related: #81 (instance 1, fixed), #262 (instance 4, inert by design), #263 (instance 3).

sample.title: Floating network maintenance sweeps every in-use address reservation three times per 30s cycle
sample.body:
## Problem

The net daemon's floating-network maintenance path re-reads every in-use address's reservation from the database three times per 30 s cycle (examined at `408fc81c6`):

- `daemons/network/maintain.py:143-144` — `for addr in fn.ipam.in_use: resv = fn.ipam.get_reservation(addr)`, and
- **two** more full per-address sweeps per `floating_ip_reaper.py` pass (lines 68 and 121),

all via `ipam.py:386` (`return mariadb.get_reservation(self.uuid, address)`), which is uncached. The rate scales with the reserved-address count, not with any work performed — the reservations being re-read are overwhelmingly standing floating-pool entries that have not changed since the previous sweep.

## Measured impact

On the sfcbr cluster (July-August 2026 DB-load measurement campaign, nightly 24h-averaged `database_requests_total` facts), `GetReservation/net` sits at a steady ~8-9 qps every day regardless of cluster activity — one of the top-three query pairs cluster-wide, effectively all of it re-reading unchanged rows.

## Suggested direction

Sweep the reservations once per maintenance cycle and share the result between the maintain pass and the two reaper passes; or batch the per-address reads into a single per-network query.

Related: the phase-5 DB-load reduction plan (#3499/#3500/#3501) and the sidechannel idle-poll fix #3595/#3596, which came from the same measurement campaign.

*(Filed with Claude Code assistance.)*

sample.title: [perf][windows] SessionStart spawns one PowerShell per cache-occupancy record; pre-tool-enforcer rebuilds the skill registry and spawns git on every tool call
sample.body:
**Version**: oh-my-claudecode 5.1.0 (plugin cache), Claude Code 2.1.x, Windows 11, Node 22. The host runs ~36 concurrent interactive Claude Code sessions (one per project) plus unattended headless runs, so anything that scales with session count or tool-call count shows up quickly.

**Summary**: two hot paths scale with session count / tool-call count on Windows. Under load they push the hooks past their 3-5 s budgets, the harness tree-kills them (`taskkill /T`, WMI work), and the host gets slower still.

### 1. SessionStart runs one PowerShell host per cache-occupancy record

- `scripts/lib/cache-occupancy.mjs:33` `identity(pid)` on win32 does `spawnSync('powershell', ['-NoProfile', '-NonInteractive', '-Command', '$p=Get-Process -Id <pid> ...; $p.StartTime...'])` with a 3 s timeout.
- `readOccupiedPluginRoots()` calls `identity()` for every registry record before any short-circuit.
- `scripts/session-start.mjs:1119` calls `readOccupiedPluginRoots(configDir)` on every SessionStart (the plugin-cache cleanup block).
- With N live sessions that each published a record, ONE SessionStart spawns up to N sequential PowerShell processes, each a full .NET host (300-900 ms on a loaded box). We measured up to 38 per SessionStart.
- `session-start.mjs` has no `DISABLE_OMC` / `OMC_SKIP_HOOKS` check, so there is no documented opt-out short of editing `hooks/hooks.json`.

Suggested fix: resolve every pid in ONE PowerShell call (`Get-Process -Id p1,p2,... | Select-Object Id,StartTime | ConvertTo-Json`), or check liveness with `process.kill(pid, 0)` first and only identity-check live pids, or cache the identity per record file behind an mtime guard. Honoring `OMC_SKIP_HOOKS` (`session-start`) there would also help.

### 2. PreToolUse `*` rebuilds the skill registry and spawns git on every tool call

- `scripts/pre-tool-enforcer.mjs:289` `buildCanonicalSkillRegistry()` re-reads every `SKILL.md` from disk on every tool call (the module-level cache cannot survive a per-call process).
- `resolveOmcRoot` (`:709`) and `resolveTranscriptPath` (`:760`) spawn `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` / `--git-common-dir`, up to 3 git spawns per call, whether or not any OMC mode is active; `readBoundedTranscript` (`:1065`) reads up to 25 MB of transcript.
- The skip guard at `:1668` only honors the token `pre-tool-use`, and skipping the whole hook also drops the model-routing and skill/agent namespace guards, so it is not a usable opt-out for cost alone.

Suggested fix: persist the registry to a JSON cache keyed by the skills directories' mtimes; skip the git spawns and the transcript read when no mode-state file exists (no active ultragoal/ralph/autopilot); make both paths lazy.

### Measurements (2026-09-05, same host)

Before mitigation: 1,514 processes, 187 `taskkill.exe`, `Win32_Process` enumeration ~900 ms, repeated `[run.cjs] Hook ... timed out after ...ms` lines. After local mitigations outside OMC (an orphaned-scan reaper, plus `OMC_SKIP_HOOKS=workflow-drift-guard,post-tool-use-failure`) the same 36 sessions sit at ~990 processes; the two items above remain the largest OMC-attributable per-session and per-call costs. `context-guard-stop.mjs` also reads the transcript on every Stop with no skip guard, a smaller version of the same pattern.

Happy to test a patch on this host.

sample.title: [DOCS] Desktop Code tab disables the CLI-native SendMessage, but the docs say cross-session messaging reaches terminal sessions
sample.body:
### Documentation Type
Incorrect/outdated documentation

### Documentation Location
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop#work-across-sessions

### Section/Topic
"Work across sessions" (desktop.md) and "Availability" (cross-session-messaging.md)

### Current Documentation

`desktop.md`, section **Work across sessions**, states:

> Cross-session messaging separately lets Claude message your other Claude Code sessions, including terminal sessions.

`cross-session-messaging.md` states:

> When a session meets the requirements, messaging is on with nothing to enable.

and its **Availability** section lists OS, provider and version requirements, plus the two documented ways to turn messaging off (permission deny rules on `SendMessage`/`ListAgents`, and `crossSessionInbound: refuse`). Neither page names the desktop app's Code tab as an exception.

### What is wrong

In the Claude desktop app (Code tab), the CLI-native `SendMessage` tool is unavailable, so a Code tab session cannot message terminal sessions at all — the opposite of what `desktop.md` promises. Two independent mechanisms in the current desktop build enforce this:

1. The app launches the Code tab session with `--disallowedTools SendMessage` (visible in `ps -ww` on the session's `claude` process; 20 of 22 live `claude` processes on this machine carry the flag).
2. The desktop bundle also registers a `PreToolUse` auto-deny for `SendMessage`, telemetry reason `cli_native_send_message`, whose message reads:

> Use `session_mgmt send_message` to message another session from the desktop app; the CLI-native `SendMessage` tool is unavailable here (terminal sessions outside Claude Desktop are not reachable from this session).

A direct call in the Code tab returns:

```
Error: No such tool available: SendMessage. SendMessage is disabled for this session, in subagents as well as here.
```

The deny message reads as deliberate product design, and the replacement it names is reasonable. The problem is that the documentation states the opposite in the one place a desktop user would look, and the Availability section — which does enumerate every other way messaging can be off — does not mention this surface at all.

### Evidence that this is surface-specific, not machine-wide

On the same machine, same Claude Code build (2.1.260), same settings, a session started from the terminal has the tool and it works:

- `claude -p ... --output-format stream-json` reports `SendMessage` and `ListAgents` in the `system/init` tool list (71 tools).
- `SendMessage` to a nonexistent recipient returns `No agent named '…' is reachable`, and `ListAgents` lists 11 peer sessions.
- Messaging a background subagent returns `{"success":true,"message":"Message queued for delivery to … at its next tool round."}` and the subagent acts on the message.

There are no `SendMessage`/`ListAgents` deny rules in user, project or local settings (verified by grep).

### Impact

Documentation-driven workflows built on `SendMessage` (waking a background subagent with a resume point, resuming agents after a limit-window reset) silently stop working when they are run from the desktop Code tab, and the docs give no way to find out why. The only explanation of the cause lives inside the deny string in the app bundle.

### Suggested fix

1. In `desktop.md` → **Work across sessions**, replace the sentence promising that cross-session messaging reaches terminal sessions with a statement that the Code tab uses the desktop's own session-messaging surface and that the CLI-native `SendMessage` is not available there.
2. In `cross-session-messaging.md` → **Availability**, add the desktop app's Code tab to the list of cases where the tools are not present, next to the deny-rule and `crossSessionInbound` entries, so `/list-agents` users can tell this case apart from a misconfiguration.

### Environment

- Claude Code 2.1.260
- Claude Desktop 1.46388.3 (the staged 1.46388.4 build contains the same deny)
- macOS (Darwin 25.6.0), Apple Silicon
- Provider: Claude subscription

sample.title: --watch: a cycle with compile-fail prints a summary indistinguishable from a clean run
sample.body:
Filed by agent impl-3, split out of #2683 so it is not closed along with it. The stale-dependency half of #2683 is fixed in #2761; this is a separate defect in the same reproduction that #2761 deliberately does not touch.

## What happens

A `--watch` cycle in which a bundle failed to compile prints a summary that is **byte-identical to a clean cycle's**, other than the `compile-fail` counter:

```
Buckets:       2 total
  ran:         1
  compile-fail:1
Tests:         54 total
  pass:        51
  fail:        3
```

54 / 51 / 3 — the same three numbers a clean run produces, because the tests that would have moved them are in the bundle that did not compile, and a test that never ran cannot fail. `=== BundleName — COMPILE FAIL ===` is printed, but roughly sixty lines above the summary block, past the per-bundle emit chatter.

## Why this one matters more than it looks

Under `--watch` **the summary is the entire interface.** There is no exit code per cycle, nobody scrolls a live watch session, and the loop's whole purpose is that a developer can glance at the bottom of the terminal and keep typing. A developer who edits, glances, and sees the same numbers as last time has no reason to look further — and every incentive not to, because the faster the loop the more it is trusted.

That is the failure mode this project keeps getting hurt by: a result that is wrong in the direction of looking fine. It is the same shape as #1904 and #2746, and the same shape as the stale-compile defect in #2683 itself, where 51 tests reported PASS against code that had been deleted.

## Possible directions, none decided

- A cycle that ends with `compile-fail > 0` could refuse to print a normal summary at all, or print the totals under a heading that cannot be mistaken for a clean run.
- The count of tests that are MISSING because their bundle did not compile is knowable (it is the previous cycle's count for that bundle) and would move a number in the direction a reader already watches.
- The interactive dashboard (`WatchDashboard`) and the plain-line fallback both need whatever the answer is; the plain-line path is the one a TUI front-end or a test harness consumes.

## Related

- #2683 — the reproduction this came out of.
- #2761 — fixes the stale-compile half; explicitly leaves this alone.
- #2762 — `EMIT-EXCLUDED` sheds objects and the run continues. Adjacent: that one is about the run's verdict, this one about the run's *display*, and a bundle can hit both in the same cycle.
- #2746 — a counted suite error whose description is printed nowhere.
- #1904 — emit-retry silently dropping AL objects.

sample.title: [Bug]: Desktop file tree shows "No project open" per-session — sticky across restart, even for sessions with identical workspace
sample.body:
## Bug Description

The Desktop right-sidebar file tree ("Files" pane) shows "未打开项目" (No project open) for some sessions while others — even ones with the **identical workspace** — show the tree correctly. The broken state survives a full app restart, and it is sticky per-session: switching to a "good" session restores the tree, switching back to a "bad" one removes it again.

Reproduced on current `main` renderer (v0.21.2, Windows 11, packaged app updated 2026-09-12 00:13 UTC).

## Repro matrix (all four sessions in ONE project lane, one profile, same state.db)

All four sessions have **identical DB workspace rows** (`sessions.cwd` = `C:\Users\WANGH\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent`, `git_branch` NULL for all, `profile_name=default`, `source=desktop`, no lineage children):

| session | created | first action this day | file tree after restart |
|---|---|---|---|
| 排查教学项目Git分支切换失效 | 09-12 08:20 | lane "+" + sent messages | ✅ tree shows |
| 修复ahk项目git丢失及文件树未打开 | 09-12 09:31 | lane "+" + sent messages | ❌ "No project open" |
| Greet user warmly | 09-12 11:47 | lane "+" + sent messages | ❌ "No project open" |
| 教学设计与组卷工具选型 | 09-12 09:17 | lane "+" (教学 lane) | (untested after restart) |

Observed behaviour (all tests after a full app restart):

1. Click "+" on the Hermes project lane → new draft → **no tree**
2. Send a message in that draft → session created (DB row has correct cwd) → **still no tree**
3. Switch to 排查教学 → **tree appears**
4. Switch back to 修复ahk / Greet → **no tree again**

Since all three rows have the same `cwd`, the discriminator is **not** the workspace path — it is the renderer's workspace-ownership claim (`$workspaceCwdOwner === $selectedStoredSessionId`, `apps/desktop/src/app/right-sidebar/index.tsx:39`).

## What the claim chain should do (and where it evidently breaks)

- Draft path: lane "+" → `startWorkspaceSession` → `startFreshSessionDraft({workspaceTarget})` → `setCurrentCwd(target)` + `setWorkspaceCwdOwner(null)`; draft owner `null === selected null` → tree should show. **Does not.**
- Create path: `createBackendSessionForSend` → `setSelectedStoredSessionId(stored)` → `applyRuntimeInfo(created.info)` → `commitWorkspaceCwdForSelectedSession(created.info.cwd)` → claim `stored === stored`. **Does not stick.**
- Switch path: `resumeSession` → `resolveStoredSession` (REST detail, full row incl. cwd) → `applyStoredSessionPreviewRuntimeInfo(stored, sid)` → claim from `stored.cwd`. Works for 排查教学, **does not** for the other two.

Verified NOT the cause:

- Backend data: `sessions.cwd` is set for all three; `GET /api/sessions` list rows include `cwd` (only `system_prompt`/`model_config`/`git_metadata_generation` are stripped); `projects.project_sessions` (entered-project view, `hydrate=true`) carries full rows.
- In-memory state: identical pattern persists across a full restart, so it is not a stale atom.

The remaining suspects are the two 09-11 renderer commits touching session-row identity/stamping (`1affcb93862` "resolve the ambient tail owner through the api/client seam", `c2d01f1012a` "key the page under the stamp its rows already carry") — both altered how cached rows are profile/connection-stamped, which feeds `resolveStoredSession`'s owner matching and the optimistic-row upsert. I could not verify the live atom values without a CDP-enabled dev build.

## Suggested investigation

Instrument `$workspaceCwdOwner` / `$selectedStoredSessionId` transitions around `openSessionTile` / `applyStoredSessionPreviewRuntimeInfo` / `applyRuntimeInfo` with the repro above; the first transition where `owner !== selected` for a row whose `cwd` is set is the bug.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11; app v0.21.2 (renderer updated 2026-09-12, commits through `1021a032569`)
- Backend: desktop-spawned `hermes serve`, single profile `default`
- Related: #108784 (same family — desktop-created sessions missing git metadata)

sample.title: Add pellet_events left after filtering other_events to intertrial response.
sample.body:
# Expose Hand Pellet Events on the Intertrial Response

_Updated: 2026-09-14 10:12 EDT_

## Objective

Add a `hand_events` property to `IntertrialResponse` carrying the pellet presentations attributed to a hand —
the exact complement of the existing `other_events`. Today those records are computed, used to produce
`food_consumed` and `successful_reaches`, and then discarded, so no consumer of the response can see the
presentations that back those counts or recompute them.

Done means: the hand-attributed pellet events reach `IntertrialResponse` alongside `other_events`, each
carrying the max frame of the reach segment it produced, the classification rule stays in the producer, and
`other_events` and its existing consumer are unchanged.

## Background

The analysis pipeline maintains two distinct event streams that are easily confused:

| Stream | Built in | One record per | Reaches the response as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pellet_events` | `_segment_reaches_f1.py:99-181` | detected pellet presentation | only the non-hand slice, as `other_events` |
| `reach_events` | `parse_pellet_presentations_jetson.py:336-498` | accepted right-hand trajectory segment | `reach_events` |

The counts split across both streams (`parse_pellet_presentations_jetson.py:511-524`): `total_reaches` is
`len(reach_events)`, while `food_consumed` and `successful_reaches` are derived from `pellet_events` and never
consult `reach_events`. The two streams also use disjoint outcome vocabularies — `EATEN` only ever appears on a
pellet event, `GRABBED`/`MISSED`/`STALLED` only ever on a reach event — so no filter over `reach_events`
reproduces `successful_reaches`.

The filter at `parse_pellet_presentations_jetson.py:193-196` keeps only the records whose `method` is neither
`RIGHT_HAND` nor `LEFT_HAND`. The discarded half is precisely the half backing `successful_reaches`. Adding it
makes `other_events` and `hand_events` a complete partition of the detected presentations, from which
`food_consumed` and `successful_reaches` become reconstructible downstream.

## Requirements

- `hand_events` holds pellet events whose `method` is `RIGHT_HAND` or `LEFT_HAND` — the strict complement of the
  `other_events` filter, so every detected presentation lands in exactly one of the two lists. Records with
  method `NONE` (a presentation never observed as lost) continue to fall to `other_events`.
- The producer stays the only place the hand/other rule is written. Ship two named lists rather than a combined
  list plus a documented rule, so no consumer re-derives the split. The rule is already duplicated once, in
  `shift_xyz_test.py:60-61`; this should not add a third copy.
- Use `ReachEvent` as the element type, sharing the `placed`/`lost` to `init`/`end` mapping and the
  `delay_since_presented` derivation `other_events` uses — including the same
  `get_t_pellet_presented_or_default()` accessor, not the direct `project.t_pellet_presented` attribute the
  reach path uses.
- `max` is the one field that does not follow `other_events`. A hand-attributed presentation involved a hand
  reach, so its record carries the real reach-max frame rather than the `-1` placeholder `other_events` uses.
  Pellet event records have no `max` today (`_segment_reaches_f1.py:128-133`), so the value has to be stamped
  onto the record inside the `segment_reaches_f2` loop, which already pairs each pellet event with the reach
  segments it produced (`parse_pellet_presentations_jetson.py:344`, and the `reach_dict` seeded from
  `pellet_event` at lines 376-383). No other correlation between a hand event and its reach segments is
  needed — `init` together with the other fields is distinguishing enough for now. The stamped value is the
  same frame index that reach segment carries as its own `max`, so a hand event and its segment agree.
- When a presentation produced more than one accepted reach segment — the search resumes after a `MISSED` or
  `STALLED` end (`parse_pellet_presentations_jetson.py:440`, `449`, `472`), while `GRABBED` and `DROPPED`
  terminate it (lines 463, 481) — `max` comes from the segment whose hand came closest to the pellet: the
  smallest `dist_hvpp_R` at that segment's own max frame. The measure is already on hand — it is what the
  acceptance filter tests at line 494 and what feeds `dist_list` at lines 441 and 470.
- When a hand-attributed presentation produced no accepted reach segment, `max` stays `None`; it does not fall
  back to `-1`. `ReachEvent.max` is `Optional[int]` documented as "None means unknown"
  (`reach_event.py:33-34`), and negative indices carry their own meaning in that type, so `-1` would be
  indistinguishable from a real pre-video frame. Nothing forces an out-of-band integer here: `hand_events` is
  not written to the reach-event HDF5 — `save_reach_events_h5()` persists `reach_events` only — and the one
  artifact the stamped records do reach, `_pelletHistory.pickle`
  (`parse_pellet_presentations_jetson.py:504-506`), round-trips `None` natively.
- A hand event's `max` can fall before its `init`. Reach search begins 20 frames ahead of placement
  (`parse_pellet_presentations_jetson.py:348`) while the record's `init` is the `placed` frame, so a segment
  that began early carries a max earlier than `init`. Consumers must not assume `init <= max <= end` on these
  records.
- Reach segmentation does not consult `method` — `frames_on_found` is appended at placement, before any method
  is known (`_segment_reaches_f1.py:127-136`) — so a presentation that ends up classified `TONGUE` or `OTHER`
  can still produce accepted reach segments. A `max` stamped onto such a record must not surface: the
  `other_events` conversion keeps its `-1` regardless, so only `hand_events` carries a real value.
- `other_events` keeps its current contents and semantics. Its one production consumer must not need changing.
- The sentinel home-position record appended at `parse_pellet_presentations_jetson.py:310-315` belongs in
  neither list;

sample.title: Prompts: Opus 5.5 practices for long unattended runs (TASKS.md checklist, when to stop, subagents, a Found section, reproducible findings)
sample.body:
## Why

Anthropic's guide [Getting the most out of Opus 5.5](https://claude.dev/blog/getting-the-most-out-of-opus-5-5) recommends a few practices for long autonomous runs. Our work steps run Claude Code `opus` unattended, and every other step runs Cursor `claude-opus-5-5-medium`. An audit of `src/prompts/*` and `src/core/step.ts` found **no thinking directives to remove** ("think carefully / step by step", "show your reasoning"): the guide says to drop those, and we have none. It also found four missing practices, listed below. All four are prompt text only; no engine logic changes.

## Change

1. **A task checklist that survives context compaction** (`src/prompts/work.md`, `github_issues/work.md`, `jira/work.md`, `sentry/work.md`). Add a step between "read the spec" and "implement": when the work has more than one part, write the parts as a checklist in `@@MEMORY_DIR@@/TASKS.md`, tick each item when it's done, and add anything new you find. Re-read it after a context summary or a resume, before doing anything else. It lives in the memory dir, never in the repo, and is never committed. Also add "read `@@MEMORY_DIR@@/TASKS.md` if it exists" to the resume nudge in `src/core/reconcile.ts` (~L2611).
2. **When to keep going and when to stop** (base belt prompt in `src/core/step.ts`, next to "Asking a human for guidance"), for every step. When a step doesn't need a human, keep going. Stop only via `ask-human` when you can't continue without one. **Never do anything destructive**: no force-push, no deleting data or branches you didn't create, no changes outside this worktree (other checkouts, `~/.config`, databases, production, published releases or tags). If the work needs one of those, `ask-human`. Panes run with permissions skipped, so the prompt is the only guard.
3. **Hand wide changes to subagents** (the work prompts, one short paragraph). When the change splits into many independent parts (a migration across many modules, an upstream merge with many conflicted files, an audit), give each part its own subagent, **check each subagent's evidence before you accept its result**, and gather the results in one table in the handoff.
4. **A `## Found` section in the handoff template** (`src/core/step.ts` ~L476). Add it after `## Uncertain`: "problems you noticed outside this step's scope (pre-existing bugs, flaky or failing tests, stale docs), each with `file:line`; omit if none". Keep the 40-line cap, with this section counted inside it. Today there is nowhere to put these, so they get lost. The article's end-of-run shape is "Blocked on me / Changed / Found": we already have ask-human for the first and `## Did` for the second.
5. **Every blocking finding says how to show it fails** (`src/prompts/review.md`, the bounce-findings paragraph). Each finding that bounces gives `file:line`, why it's wrong, and **how to show it fails**: a command, a test, or input → wrong output. The work step can then reproduce it before fixing, and the loop converges faster. Don't change what bounces.

Update `docs/PROMPTS.md` / `skills/herdr-factory/references/prompts.md` wherever they describe these prompts or the handoff template.

## Done when

- the prompt snapshot or render tests cover the new text, and the suite passes;
- `herdr-factory --repo <any github repo> prompts` renders the work prompt with the TASKS.md step, the subagent paragraph and the stop/destructive rule, and the handoff template contains `## Found`;
- `git grep -n -i -E "think (carefully|hard|step)|step[- ]by[- ]step" src/prompts` still returns nothing.

sample.title: Code review: packages/ai/src/auth/oauth/openai-codex.ts
sample.body:
# Code Review: packages/ai/src/auth/oauth/openai-codex.ts - OpenAI Codex OAuth (440 lines)

## File Analysis

`openai-codex.ts` implements the OpenAI Codex (ChatGPT Plus/Pro) OAuth
flow with two login methods: browser (PKCE + localhost callback) and
device code (headless). The file uses a fire-and-forget module-level
`import("node:crypto")` / `import("node:http")` pattern to avoid
breaking browser/Vite builds. The file has **one critical race
condition** and several other real issues.

### Race conditions: 2

1. **Module-level fire-and-forget `import()` is racy** (lines 11-19):

   ```typescript
   let _randomBytes: typeof import("node:crypto").randomBytes | null = null;
   let _http: typeof import("node:http") | null = null;
   if (typeof process !== "undefined" && (process.versions?.node || process.versions?.bun)) {
       import("node:crypto").then((m) => {
           _randomBytes = m.randomBytes;
       });
       import("node:http").then((m) => {
           _http = m;
       });
   }
   ```

   The `import()` calls return promises that are NEVER awaited.
   `createState()` (line 86) and `startLocalOAuthServer()` (line 320)
   check `_randomBytes !== null` / `_http !== null` synchronously. If
   `loginOpenAICodex` is called before the dynamic imports resolve
   (cold start, fast test runner, dynamic import via `load.ts`), the
   checks fail and the user sees the misleading error `"OpenAI Codex
   OAuth is only available in Node.js environments"` even on Node.
   Fix: make `createState` and `startLocalOAuthServer` async and
   `await import("node:crypto")` / `await import("node:http")` at the
   top of each. Or use static imports gated by an `if` block at module
   init (the `process.versions?.bun` check already gates Node-only code).

2. **`server.close()` in finally may race with in-flight `listen`**
   (line 396, 401). If the user cancels between `server.listen(1455,
   getCallbackHost(), ...)` scheduling and the listen callback firing,
   `server.close()` runs in `finally` before the listen resolves. The
   close throws `ERR_SERVER_NOT_RUNNING`. The promise from
   `startLocalOAuthServer` then resolves with a server that's already
   closed; `waitForCode` never resolves and the user sees a hang. Add
   a `server.once("close", ...)` listener and check `server.listening`
   before calling close.

### UX/UI observations: 4

1. **No browser auto-launch** (line 387). The notify text reads
   `"A browser window should open. Complete login to finish."` — but
   nothing in this file (or the call site) opens the browser. Users
   who don't notice the URL in their terminal have no affordance to
   open it. Either auto-launch via the existing `open-browser` utility
   (referenced elsewhere in the repo) or change the copy to `"Open
   this URL in your browser: ${url}"` so the contract is honest.

2. **Device-code 403/404 is treated as "pending"** (lines 213-215):
   ```typescript
   if (response.status === 403 || response.status === 404) {
       return { status: "pending" };
   }
   ```
   If OpenAI's server starts returning 403 for an invalidated
   `device_auth_id` (e.g., expired between phases), the user sees an
   indefinite spinner instead of "this device code is no longer
   valid". Distinguish 403-rejected (fail fast) from 403-pending (retry).

3. **Hard-coded `REDIRECT_URI` ignores `PI_OAUTH_CALLBACK_HOST`** (line 17).
   Same bug as #735 UX #1: the env var `PI_OAUTH_CALLBACK_HOST`
   changes the listen host, but `REDIRECT_URI` always says
   `http://localhost:1455/auth/callback`. Anthropic's docs
   (https://auth.openai.com) will register the localhost URL, but the
   server listens on the env-configured host, so the browser redirect
   never lands. The redirect URI must be derived from the same source
   as the listen host.

4. **No timeout on the OAuth callback server** (line 320). If the
   user closes their browser without completing, `server.waitForCode()`
   never resolves; `interaction.signal` only aborts if the surrounding
   flow cancels. Add a 5-minute `setTimeout(() => settleWait(null),
   5 * 60_000)` matching the same fix in #735 (anthropic.ts).

### Code-review observations: 5

1. **Two separate `import()` calls for `node:crypto` + `node:http`**
   (lines 15, 18). Combine via `Promise.all` to halve the round-trips:

   ```typescript
   Promise.all([import("node:crypto"), import("node:http")]).then(([crypto, http]) => {
       _randomBytes = crypto.randomBytes;
       _http = http;
   });
   ```

2. **`createState` only uses 16 bytes of entropy** (line 89).
   `randomBytes(16).toString("hex")` is 32 hex chars = 128 bits, which
   is sufficient for OAuth state. RFC 6749 §10.10 recommends ≥128
   bits; 32 bytes (256 bits) is the conventional default and costs
   nothing. Bump to `randomBytes(32)` for headroom.

3. **`refreshAccessToken` has no per-request timeout** (lines 167-185).
   `exchangeAuthorizationCode` uses the caller's signal but no
   timeout; `refreshAccessToken` does the same. Both can hang
   indefinitely on a stalled connection. Wrap with
   `AbortSignal.any([signal, AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)])` for
   symmetry with `resolveStoredOAuth` in `auth/resolve.ts`.

4. **`fetchWithLoginCancellation` swallows the original abort reason**
   (lines 116-124):
   ```typescript
   if (init.signal?.aborted) {
       throw new Error("Login cancelled");
   }
   ```
   The new `Error` has no `cause` and discards `signal.reason`.
   Forward the original abort reason so callers can distinguish
   "user cancelled" from "signal aborted because refresh timed out":

   ```typescript
   if (init.signal?.aborted) {
       throw new Error("Login cancelled", { cause: init.signal.reason });
   }
   ```

5. **Hard-coded port `1455`** (line 17, 350) and magic number
   `DEVICE_CODE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 15 * 60` (line 21) sit at module
   scope alongside the other URL constants. Extract a `const
   OAUTH_CONFIG = { port: 1455, timeoutSeconds: 15 * 60, ... }` so
   the OAuth server config

sample.title: docs(idd-ci): broaden Wake-up discipline's scope sentence beyond CI/bot review
sample.body:
<!-- idd-skill-authoring-publication: target=target-e75a9933e5016993; anchor=kurone-kito/idd-skill#2843; set=set-0a071ee0641b88b6; session=claude-sonnet5-95c4e29c82659dc7; token=pub-20b8fe1b6610d4da -->

## Background

`.github/instructions/idd-ci.instructions.md`'s "Wake-up discipline"
section opens by scoping itself in prose to "a session pushing a commit
and waiting on CI or bot review outside a formal IDD claim too" (line
330-332, unchanged since 2026-09-03). It never says the section also
covers a **local** build/test/lint wait, even though the section's own
operative guidance already does: `idd-skill#2798` (merged via PR #2811,
closed 2026-09-09) added "Never blindly re-issue a heavy local command (a
full build, test, or lint run) that auto-backgrounds past the tool's
default timeout ... Check whether the prior invocation is still running
first ... then await/reap it or reuse its eventual result" about 30 lines
below that opening sentence.

A field-feedback gist reported two independent delegated workers, on two
different issues in the same session, each ending its turn assuming a
completion notification would resume it after a local Pester run got
auto-backgrounded past the calling tool's own timeout -- the exact
failure `#2798`'s text now addresses in substance. Their session was
pinned to `idd-skill` `v0.9.0` (tagged 2026-09-06), which predates
`#2798` (closed 2026-09-09), so the concrete incident itself already
has a fix on `main`. The one residual gap is that the section's own
topic sentence still doesn't name local waits as in-scope, so a reader
who only skims the intro (rather than the full section) could still
misjudge scope and stop reading before reaching the now-existing local-
command guidance.

## Proposed change

Broaden the "Wake-up discipline" section's opening scope sentence (or add
a short adjoining clause) to name any long-running foreground command a
phase requires -- CI polling, bot/advisory review waits, and local
build/test/lint runs alike -- as in-scope, rather than leaving scope
implicit until a reader reaches the local-command bullet several
paragraphs later. Keep the existing local-command guidance
(`#2798`'s addition) unchanged; this is a scope-statement clarity fix
only, not a new behavioral rule.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Wake-up discipline section's opening prose explicitly names local
  build/test/lint waits as in scope, alongside CI and bot/advisory
  review waits, rather than only listing the latter two.
- No change to the section's existing local-command recovery guidance
  (the `#2798` addition) beyond what is needed for the scope sentence to
  read consistently with it.
- `node scripts/audit-docs.mjs --check` (or the profile-equivalent)
  still passes after the edit.

## Candidate files

- `idd-template/.github/instructions/idd-ci.instructions.md`
- `.github/instructions/idd-ci.instructions.md` (regenerated via
  `node scripts/sync-docs.mjs --apply`, not hand-edited directly)

scope-sentence edit with a fully specified wording direction._

sample.title: Make the apps/docs conventions enforceable, and fix what drifted
sample.body:
Most of `apps/docs` is in good shape. Greps for every banned word and phrase in `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` return almost nothing across 40 pages: no "simply", no "allows you to", no "we", no "users", no unspaced em dashes, no unresolved internal links, no missing example targets. The problems are stale generated output, a handful of wrong statements, and the same content written three or four times.

## Why it drifted

The violations split cleanly along whether a rule is enforced.

Rules that `component-doc-contract.ts` checks had **zero** violations across 26 component guides. Rules that exist only as prose in DOCUMENTATION.md drifted on most pages. A test result arrives as feedback while the work is happening. A rule at line 340 of a 421-line guide has to be recalled.

Two things make this worse:

1. `pnpm run check` excludes tests, and root AGENTS.md says so explicitly. So the entire docs enforcement layer sits outside the loop agents are told to run before committing.
2. The docs CI job runs `pnpm --filter docs run generate` and then `run test`, so it regenerates the Props pages before asserting anything about them. The drift test can never see stale committed files.

Astro's contribution guide can afford to be prose, because a docs team is the enforcement layer. We do not have one, so the test suite has to be it.

## What is actually wrong

Four things are broken:

1. **All 24 committed `props.mdx` files are stale.** Every `auto-type-table` path points at a file that no longer exists, using the pre-move layout (`src/button/index.tsx`, `src/text-field/primitive/*`) while the guides declare the current one. 38 distinct paths, none present on disk. `generate-props-pages.test.ts` fails locally today. The deployed site is fine, because `build` depends on `generate`.
2. **`docs/token-reference.mdx` documents a breakpoint that does not exist.** Lines 35 and 38 use `xsmall`, and `breakpoints.ts` has no such key. `docs/layout.mdx` states the real list correctly, so the two pages contradict each other and the snippet would not typecheck. This is the class of error the "prefer a typechecked `ExampleBlock`" rule exists to prevent.
3. **`VisuallyHidden` is documented as a primitive.** It exports from `@luke-ui/react/visually-hidden`, not `primitives/*`.
4. **`combobox-field.mdx:19` sends readers to a component that does not exist**, telling them to "use another component for multiple selection".

Two sections should not be there at all. `components/visuals/icon.mdx` breaks four rules in one place: it documents the `<svg>` and `<use>` mechanism that DOCUMENTATION.md line 56 names as its canonical example of what to cut, restates the Props page as a bullet list, uses `myIcon` and `tomato` where the guide requires realistic values, and explains that `aria-hidden={false}` has no effect, which is an unsupported path. Separately, `docs/color.mdx:106-133` is a 28-line migration guide with a 10-row table for `color.intent`, an API that no longer exists in any form. The page even says there is nothing to fall back on.

Then there is duplication. Six examples are referenced from two pages each, five of them under a different title on each page, and every pair is also a prose duplication. Shared examples turn out to be a reliable detector for the wider problem, which is eight topics written on two to four pages each.

Underneath all of it, four conventions were never pinned down, which is why each page resolved them differently: the heading name for cross-reference sections (four variants in use), `## Best practices` (named in the guide, used by no page), closing navigation on authored guides (three variants), and whether generated MDX is committed.

## Decisions

Settled in a grilling session. Recorded here so the work does not relitigate them.

The architecture is two layers. A new `apps/docs/scripts/check-docs.ts` owns every mechanically checkable rule, following the shape `check-story-plays.ts` already uses. DOCUMENTATION.md owns the judgement and explains why each rule exists, without restating what the script checks, so the two cannot drift apart.

Generated MDX stops being committed. Turbo already declares `content/docs/components/*/*/props.mdx` and `meta.json` as `docs#generate` outputs, and `dev`, `test`, `build`, and `check:format` all depend on `generate`, so nothing reads the committed copies. Guide and Props frontmatter parity then holds by construction.

Docs conformance moves into `check`, as a `check:docs` task, so the loop AGENTS.md prescribes actually covers docs.

Component guides get a closed H2 set: `## Best practices`, then feature sections, then `## Accessibility`, then `## Related components`, with `## Anatomy` allowed on primitives. Order is enforced for the fixed sections and free for feature sections. `## Primitive` folds into `## Related components`, because two names means classifying every link before writing the heading. `## Best practices` becomes the canonical name and the pages move to it. `## Accessibility` is required for actions, forms, and feedback, and optional elsewhere. Authored guides stay free-form apart from a required `## Continue learning` with `<Cards>`, which is forbidden on component guides.

A small subset of the prose rules gets pattern-matched across MDX and `docs/*.md`: no prose semicolons, no "assistive technologies", em dash spacing, the banned filler list, and forbidden terminology. Code fences are stripped before matching, and no pattern that can produce a false positive goes in. The writing-style rules now bind the internal guides too, while the surface-scope rules stay separate, because their reader genuinely differs.

For AI authorship, `components/actions/button.mdx` is named in the guide as the canonical exemplar, on the reasoning that a real page cannot rot into fiction. A short authoring checklist goes at the top of DOCUMENTATION.md, with the existing editorial sections kept as the reference behind it. The hand-maintained generator list comes out

sample.title: How is a stale or dead agent noticed?
sample.body:
Part of #1813

## Question

The failure path, per harness and model source: an expired subscription login, a hit budget cap, an exhausted rate window, a trigger bridge that stopped receiving, a run that errored. Each must notify on the channel the affected alert or episode would have used, marked as an error, with the raw error text. Liveness: the always-firing Watchdog alert routed through the trigger bridge on a no-op path, a `last_success_timestamp` metric, a staleness rule plus an `absent()` twin (#1575 part 4 already sketches this).

## Resolve by

Grilling. Resolution: the list of failure modes with their signal, and the liveness design.

sample.title: openapi codegen genruns analyzed under two exec configs, causing avoidable remote-cache misses in CI
sample.body:
## Summary

The OpenAPI-generated client genruns (e.g. `//generated/py/manman:worker_dal_api_tar_gen`, and siblings like `experience_api_tar_gen`, `status_api_tar_gen`, defined via the `openapi_client` macro in `tools/openapi/openapi_client_rule.bzl:98-133`) appear to re-execute on effectively every `test` job run in CI, even though the remote cache is live and healthy (~65% hit rate in the run this was noticed in) and the rule itself is fully deterministic.

Log example from a `test` job run: https://github.com/whale-net/everything/actions/runs/33941988757/job/101241096921#step:4:212 — `openapi-generator-cli` regenerating `manman_worker_dal_api` from scratch.

## Root cause (confirmed)

This is **not** a caching/determinism problem with the rule itself:
- No `no-cache`/`no-remote-cache`/`local` tags on the genrule (only `tags = ["openapi"]`).
- `stamp = 0` is already set specifically to avoid volatile build-info invalidation (see the "Force deterministic caching" comment at the rule definition).
- Building the target directly and re-running gives an instant `up-to-date` (0.31s, zero re-execution) — a normal, cacheable action in isolation.

The actual cause: within a full `bazel coverage --build_tests_only //...` (or `//...`) invocation, this same genrule (and its upstream `//manman:worker-dal-api_openapi_spec` generator) is analyzed under **two different exec configurations** — visible in the log as two distinct `bazel-out/k8-opt-exec-ST-<hash>/...` output paths for the same target. Each distinct exec config has its own action cache key, so one of the two forks is often a cold remote-cache miss on a given run even though the *other* fork hits cache fine. Building the target in isolation only ever produces one config (`k8-fastbuild`), so this fork only shows up when the full `//...` graph is walked — something else reachable from `//...` is very plausibly pulling this genrule in under an ARM64 cross-compilation exec transition (see `docs/DOCKER.md` — this repo uses true cross-compilation for ARM64, and breakage/duplication here is easy to introduce silently).

## Recommended next step

Identify exactly what forces the second exec configuration:

```
bazel cquery --transitions=full //generated/py/manman:worker_dal_api_tar_gen --config=ci //...
```

or

```
bazel aquery 'mnemonic("Genrule", //generated/py/manman:worker_dal_api_tar_gen)' --config=ci //...
```

against the full `//...` universe (not just the target in isolation) to find the consumer that depends on this genrule under a non-default exec platform. Once found, decide whether that consumer genuinely needs a platform-specific instance of the OpenAPI-generated client (unlikely — it's just generated Python source) or can be pointed at the shared/default-exec-config instance instead, collapsing the two forks into one cacheable action.

**Read `docs/DOCKER.md` before touching anything here** — this repo's cross-compilation setup fails silently at build time and only breaks at runtime, per `AGENTS.md`'s critical-path warning.

## Separate, lower-priority note (same investigation, different issue)

`tools/openapi/openapi_gen_wrapper.sh` (lines ~7-18) prefers the system `java` on `PATH` over the Bazel-toolchain-provided `$(JAVA)` from the declared `toolchains = ["@bazel_tools//tools/jdk:current_java_runtime"]` toolchain, skipping the toolchain arg via `shift`. The actual Java binary/version used isn't a declared Bazel input, so if the system JDK ever differs between machines (local dev vs. a future CI runner image bump), Bazel has no way to know to invalidate the cache — a correctness risk in the *opposite* direction (stale/wrong cache reuse) from this issue's main topic. Worth a follow-up but is not the cause of the doubling above.

🤖 Filed by [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

sample.title: [Zdtp 0.5 Adoption][Epic] Adopt zdtp 0.5.0 and close the prior integration loop
sample.body:
## Goal

Adopt `@takazudo/zdtp` 0.5.0 completely after the 0.4.15 integration round: update every pin, consume the new side-effect-free constants API, add the package-default preview metadata upstream is waiting on, resolve the Color-persistence documentation contradiction, and prove the two reported UI problems are gone in the real zudo-doc consumer.

**Parent branch:** `main`
**Base branch:** `base/zdtp-0-5-0-adoption`
**Plan mode:** goal-clear

## Verified upstream impact

- Current `0.4.15`; target `0.5.0` from npm `latest`.
- Two registry rows require updates; 13 first-party dependency rows are current and two workspace specs remain skipped.
- npm omits `gitHead`, but verified tags `v0.4.15` (`34c2610f`) and `v0.5.0` (`da9d4a63`) form a linear 19-commit range; published tarballs were compared directly.
- Existing exports, Preact peer `^10.29.1`, and Node/pnpm engines are unchanged. The additive `@takazudo/zdtp/constants` leaf is import-free and 990 bytes.
- 0.5.0 fixes unreadably collapsed changed-token labels and inaccessible compact dock escape controls.
- `Takazudo/zudo-design-token-panel#766` (320px unchanged-tier overflow) and `Takazudo/zudo-design-token-panel#770` (700px header overflow) remain open and are not part of the 0.5.0 fix.
- No `ZUDO_DEPS_PINS.md` exists and no vendored artifact needs syncing.

## Delegated decisions

1. Consume `@takazudo/zdtp/constants` now instead of re-dating local mirrors. The built graph must show only the constants leaf is eager; the panel payload stays dynamic.
2. Preserve zudo-doc's deliberate `:autoload="auto"` exception. The upstream reference accepts `"auto"`; this consumer continues to eager-load only explicit owner value `"1"`.
3. Adopt exact state-family matching and `requiredConfig` metadata. This corrects raw-empty-string, junk-suffix, and DOM Tweaker false-positive behavior with explicit tests.
4. Add the preview metadata requested by `Takazudo/zudo-design-token-panel#699`. Do not add `dock.reflow` without direct fixed-header evidence.
5. Resolve #3980: the package builder already declares distinct Default Light/Dark identities, so the reference page is correct and the guide plus `src/CLAUDE.md` are stale. Prove it in-browser and close through the root PR.
6. Keep #3978 and #3979 outside this dependency task; they are unrelated. Generated files from #3979 must not enter commits.

## Execution graph

Wave numbers are informational; `Depends on` gates scheduling. Chromium-heavy work is serialized by a real dependency edge.

| Wave | Sub-task | Depends on | Execution mode | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [#3982](https://github.com/zudolab/zudo-doc/issues/3982) Bump all zdtp pins and lockfile | none | subagents - bounded dependency update | standard - deterministic resolver and known pin surfaces |
| 2 | [#3984](https://github.com/zudolab/zudo-doc/issues/3984) Adopt isolated constants and exact gate metadata | #3982 | subagents - bootstrap correctness work | high - subtle lazy graph and persistence behavior |
| 2 | [#3983](https://github.com/zudolab/zudo-doc/issues/3983) Add preview metadata | #3982 | subagents - localized manifest work | standard - complete upstream mapping exists |
| 2 | [#3985](https://github.com/zudolab/zudo-doc/issues/3985) Lock mode-scoped Color persistence and resolve #3980 | #3982 | subagents - browser contract plus bilingual docs | high - persisted identity behavior needs empirical proof |
| 3 | [#3986](https://github.com/zudolab/zudo-doc/issues/3986) Verify 0.5 UI fixes in zudo-doc | #3985 (resource edge) | subagents - focused browser regression | high - pointer and responsive geometry can be falsely green |
| 4 | [#3987](https://github.com/zudolab/zudo-doc/issues/3987) Confirm integrated adoption and repository gates | #3984, #3983, #3986 | subagents - final merged-base gate | standard - known repository commands |

## Acceptance

- All three zdtp pin surfaces and `pnpm-lock.yaml` use 0.5.0; no unrelated lockfile churn.
- The bootstrap consumes the public constants leaf, preserves the autoload provenance policy, and no longer mirrors names/state-family rules from minified bundles.
- The package-default manifest exposes the preview metadata required by `Takazudo/zudo-design-token-panel#699`.
- Browser evidence proves Color is mode-scoped, non-color tabs remain global, changed-row labels are readable, and right-docked users can escape through pointer-accessible controls at compact widths.
- Existing `Takazudo/zudo-design-token-panel#766` / `Takazudo/zudo-design-token-panel#770` behavior is checked and recorded without a consumer workaround.
- Fresh smoke/theme E2E fixtures, workspace build, checks/tests, lazy graph inspection, and `pnpm b4push` pass.
- Root PR targets `main` and contains `Closes #3980`.

The parent baseline is trusted green from PR #3977's complete CI matrix; a local package baseline also passes 252 files / 2,861 tests. Disk headroom is 646 GiB.

sample.title: review: no honest candidate exists for reviewing already-merged SDD change content
sample.body:
### Problem Description

The review facade derives its review candidate from the repository workspace's current changes. For an SDD change whose implementation was **already merged to the main branch** (delivered via chained PRs in sessions where native review was unavailable), there is no honest candidate left to review:

- `gentle-ai review status --contract gentle-ai.review-integration/v2 --next-transition` returns `next_transition.kind=execute` with `review.start --projection=workspace` bound to a target whose only paths are **unrelated untracked files** (user notes folder). Starting that review would bind review authority to a candidate that contains none of the change's content — authority laundering.
- `gentle-ai review bind-sdd` requires `--lineage` from an **existing** review lineage for the change; none exists for never-natively-reviewed work, and binding a foreign change's lineage would misattribute review authority.
- `gentle-ai review recover` requires predecessor/successor lineages (lineage chaining, not initial minting for merged content).
- `gentle-ai review capabilities` fails safely with `operation_failed` (pre_native).

Result: a completed, verified, merged SDD change **cannot be closed through the native review/archive gate** — the only honest exits are leaving the change open forever or a manual authorized filesystem archive without a review receipt.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deliver an SDD change fully merged to `main` with no native review receipt (e.g. review was unavailable during delivery).
2. Run `gentle-ai sdd-status <change> --json` → `nextRecommended: resolve-review`, `blockedReasons: ["compact review authority is not bound to selected change ..."]`.
3. Run `gentle-ai review status --contract gentle-ai.review-integration/v2 --next-transition` → the returned `review.start` transition targets only unrelated untracked workspace files.
4. Attempt every binding/recovery operation (`bind-sdd`, `recover`, `repair`) — none can mint authority for the merged content.

### Expected Behavior

A provider-supported way to mint review authority for an already-merged change's content, e.g.:
- a change-scoped projection that reviews `base_tree → merged_tree` for the change's paths (derived from the SDD runtime ledger / openspec artifacts), or
- a `bind-sdd` mode that accepts the change's runtime evidence and starts a review over the merged tree pair instead of the live workspace.

### Actual Behavior

No honest native input exists; the transition offers a review of unrelated workspace noise. Teams must fall back to manual authorized archives (documented precedent in our repo: `frontend-admin`, `resident-read-endpoints`, `frontend-resident`), losing the review receipt leg of the gate.

### Operating System

macOS

### Agent / Client

OpenCode

### Shell

zsh

### Relevant Logs

```json
{"applicability":"unrelated","action":"start","reason_code":"fresh_target_ready",
 "projection":{"kind":"current-changes","projection":"workspace",
 "paths":["Dudas y consultas/.atl/.skill-registry.cache.json","Dudas y consultas/.atl/skill-registry.md"]}}
```

### Additional Context

The SDD runtime ledger side works perfectly for this scenario: `sdd-attempt reset` (maintainer-authorized) + `begin`/`finish` charged a fresh `verify-change-wide` attempt that passed with validator-admitted evidence. The gap is only on the review-authority side.
